By Order in Council, O.C. 1774/85, the Lieutenant-Governor in Council, pursuant to s. 19 of the Courts of Justice Act, 1984 (Ont.), c. 11, referred the following question to the Ontario Court of Appeal, for its opinion:
"Is Bill 30, An Act to amend the Education Act [to provide full funding for Roman Catholic separate high schools] inconsistent with the provisions of the Constitution of Canada including the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
and, if so, in what particular or particulars and in what respect?"
Answer by the court (Howland C.J.O. and Robins J.A. dissenting): Bill 30 is not inconsistent with the provisions of the Constitution of Canada.
Per Zuber, Cory and Tarnopolsky JJ.A.: The Constitution of Canada, which by virtue of
s. 52(2)
of the
Constitution Act, 1982
, includes, inter alia, the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the
British North America Act, 1867
(renamed the Constitution Act, 1867), has from the beginning provided for group collective rights in
ss. 93
and
133
of the Constitution Act, 1867. These provisions amount to "a small bill of rights". The provisions of this "small bill of rights", now expanded as to the language rights of
s. 133
by
ss. 16
to
23
of the Charter, constitute a major difference from a bill of rights such as that of the United States, which is based on individual rights. Collective or group rights, such as those concerning language in
s. 133
and those concerning rights of certain denominations to separate schools in
s. 93
, are asserted by individuals or groups of individuals because of their membership in the protected group. Individual rights are asserted equally by everyone despite membership in certain ascertainable groups. Collective rights protect certain groups and not others. To that extent, they are an exception to the equality rights provided equally to everyone. Thus, a court cannot rely upon
s. 15
of the Charter to invalidate a provision for the English or French languages, guaranteed pursuant to ss. 16 to 23 of the Charter, on the ground that such provision does not provide for equal protection or benefit to another language.
The provision in
s. 93
of the
Constitution Act, 1867
for the rights of Protestants and Roman Catholics to separate schools became part of "a small bill of rights" as a basic compact of Confederation. The reciprocity of the protection was built into s. 93(2). A literal interpretation of that provision would lead one to conclude that dissentient schools in the new Quebec were to be given the same protection as the Roman Catholics had by law in Upper Canada at the Union. In Quebec this has been interpreted and applied as giving rights to public funding for separate schools, including the secondary school level, up to university entrance standards. In Ontario, s. 93 has never been applied so as to provide full funding for separate secondary schools. The issue of separate high school funding has been attended with difficulties, opposition and, not infrequently, with litigation. In this light, the purpose of Bill 30 must be seen as an attempt to redress an historical grievance and to remove a continuing irritant in relations with Quebec.
By s. 93, the provincial legislatures were granted plenary power over education subject only to the legal restrictions of s-s. 93(1) and to the possibility, never realized, of being overridden by action of the Governor-General in Council and the Parliament of Canada under s-ss. 93(3) and (4). Therefore, at least at any time prior to the coming into force of the
Charter
and of
s. 15
thereof, there was nothing in s. 93 that would have prevented the provincial Legislature from providing for full funding of Roman Catholic separate high schools, unless it could be shown that such law would, in the words of s. 93(1), "prejudicially affect any Right or Privilege with respect to Denominational Schools which any Class of Persons have by Law in the Province at the Union". No such prejudice has been or could be shown.
The key
Charter
provision is
s. 29
. It provides that "Nothing in this Charter abrogates or derogates from any rights or privileges guaranteed by or under the Constitution of Canada in respect of denominational, separate or dissentient schools." If s. 29 was intended to protect only constitutional rights and privileges from the Charter, the words "by virtue of any provision of the Constitution of Canada" might have been expected to be used instead of "by or under the Constitution of Canada". The words "under the Constitution of Canada" must include rights and privileges granted by laws enacted under the authority of the Constitution. That this was the intention of the framers of the Constitution Act, 1982, is clear from the Proceedings and Evidence of the Special Joint Committee of the Senate and of the House of Commons on the Constitution of Canada, 1980-81, which show that s. 29 was intended to protect not only "any rights or privileges guaranteed by ... the Constitution of Canada", such as those in
s. 93
of the
Constitution Act, 1867
, s. 17 of each of the Alberta Act, 1905 (Can.), c. 3, and the Saskatchewan Act, 1905 (Can.), c. 42, and Term 17 of the Terms of Union of Newfoundland with Canada (Newfoundland Act, 1949 (U.K.), c. 22), but also "any rights or privileges guaranteed ... under the Constitution of Canada", such as those contained within provincial statutes enacted pursuant to the plenary power over education in the opening paragraph of
s. 93
. Bill 30, if enacted, would be one such statute and so must, at least in its basic purpose and over-all thrust, receive the protection of s. 29 from any abrogation or derogation because of any of the rights or freedoms set out in the Charter, including
ss. 2(a)
and
15
.
The answer, therefore, to the question referred to the court is that Bill 30, in its basic purpose and over-all thrust, is not "inconsistent with the provisions of the Constitution of Canada including the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
". This conclusion does not mean that separate schools are exempt from the law or the Constitution. Laws and the Constitution, particularly the Charter, are excluded from application to separate schools only to the extent that they derogate from such schools as Roman Catholic (or in Quebec, Protestant) institutions. It is this essential Roman Catholic nature which is preserved and protected by s. 93 of the Constitution and
s. 29
of the Charter. The courts must strike a balance, on a case- by-case basis, between conduct essential to the proper functioning of the Roman Catholic schools and conduct which contravenes such Charter rights as those of equality in
s. 15
or of conscience and religion in
s. 2(a)
.
Per Howland C.J.O. and Robins J.A. dissenting: It is true that
s. 93(1)
of the
Constitution Act, 1867
represents a fundamental Confederation bargain. However, the rights or privileges guaranteed Roman Catholics by this section are limited to those which they had by law at the time of Confederation. These rights or privileges must be strictly honoured. But the guarantee is limited to funding for elementary education and does not include full funding of Roman Catholic separate schools. Bill 30 does not confer a right or privilege guaranteed to Roman Catholic separate schools by or under the Constitution and is not immune from
Charter
scrutiny. Section 29 only applies to rights and privileges in respect of separate schools which are guaranteed. In Ontario the rights and privileges under
s. 93(1)
are the only ones which fall in this category.
Prior to the coming into force of the
Charter
, Bill 30 would have been a valid exercise of provincial legislative authority. However, the Charter as part of Canada's Constitution establishes a new relationship between the individual and the State. Its text marks the metes and bounds of government authority and individual autonomy. Bill 30 is inconsistent with
s. 15(1)
of the Charter which gives to every individual the right to equal benefit of the law without discrimination based on religion. If this right is to mean anything, it must mean at least that the followers of one religion are not to be the beneficiaries of greater benefits provided by law than the followers of other religions. Bill 30 provides benefits on the basis of religion to one religious group only and is therefore in direct conflict with this right. Nor has Bill 30 been justified as a reasonable limit under
s. 1
of the Charter. Although one can sympathize with Roman Catholic parents who must pay both public school taxes and denominational school fees, the same holds true for members of other religions who send their children to religious schools. Ontario today is a multicultural and pluralistic society composed of people of many diverse social, ethnic, racial and religious backgrounds. Religion is a dominant feature of their multicultural heritage and, by the very terms of
s. 27
of the Charter, the multicultural heritage of Canadians is to be preserved and enhanced. Therefore, Bill 30 is unconstitutional and would be of no force or effect if enacted.

HOWLAND C.J.O. and ROBINS J.A. (dissenting):-- Pursuant to
the Courts of Justice Act, 1984 (Ont.), c. 11, s. 19, the
Lieutenant-Governor in Council by Order in Council, O.C. 1774/
85, dated July 3, 1985, referred to this Court for hearing
and consideration the following question:

Is Bill 30, an Act to amend the Education Act inconsistent
with the provisions of the Constitution of Canada including
the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
and, if so, in
what particular or particulars and in what respect?

By order of the Chief Justice of Ontario, upon application for
directions made by the Attorney-General for Ontario, notice of
the reference was given to the Attorney-General of Canada and
by publication in various newspapers in circulation in Ontario.
The intervenants who appeared by counsel or in person at the
hearing to make oral representations did so pursuant to the Act
and the terms of the notice.

In addition to the intervenants who made oral
representations, written respresentations were received on
behalf of the Canadian Unitarian Council and the Policy
Analysis and Research Management both of whom opposed the
constitutionality of Bill 30.

At the outset of the hearing, the Chief Justice of Ontario
pointed out that the sole question for this Court to determine
was the constitutionality of Bill 30 and that it was not the
role of this Court to determine on this reference whether or
not the provision of full funding under Bill 30 should await
its decision.

For the sake of convenience, we begin by setting out the
general format of our reasons:

I. Summary of position taken in dissent
II. Historical development of the school system in Ontario
A.  Pre-Confederation development
B.  Section 93 of the Constitution Act, 1867
C.  Post-Confederation history
The Tiny case
Historical developments since the Tiny case
D.  Bill 30
III. The proper interpretation of s. 93
IV. Binding effect of the Tiny case
V. Is Bill 30 shielded from scrutiny under the
Charter
by s.
29?
VI. Is Bill 30 inconsistent with
s. 2(a)
or
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter?
VII. Can Bill 30 be saved by
s. 1
of the Charter?
VIII. Conclusion

I.  SUMMARY OF POSITION TAKEN IN DISSENT

The main argument of those who support the constitutionality
of Bill 30 is that full funding of Roman Catholic separate
schools is a right or privilege within the meaning of
s. 93(1)

of the
Constitution Act, 1867
. That section prevents the
Legislature from prejudicially affecting certain rights or
privileges of Roman Catholic separate schools. The proponents
of Bill 30 contend therefore that its provisions cannot be
challenged under the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
,
by reason of
s. 29
of the Charter which, in the context of this
reference, provides that nothing in the Charter abrogates or
derogates from any right or privilege guaranteed to Roman
Catholic separate schools by or under the Constitution. We
reject this submission. We do agree that
s. 93(1)
represents a
fundamental Confederation bargain. However, the rights or
privileges guaranteed to Roman Catholics by this section are
limited to those which they had by law at the time of
Confederation. These rights or privileges must be strictly
honoured. But the guarantee is limited to funding for
elementary education and does not include full funding of Roman
Catholic separate schools. This was decided almost 60 years ago
by the Privy Council in Tiny Separate School Trustees v. The
King (1926),
1927 CanLII 9 (SCC)
, 59 O.L.R. 96; affirmed
1926 CanLII 364 (ON SCAD)
, 60 O.L.R. 15, [1927] 1
D.L.R. 913; affirmed [1927] S.C.R. 637, [1927] 4 D.L.R. 857;
affirmed
1928 CanLII 355 (UK JCPC)
, [1928] 3 D.L.R. 753, [1928] A.C. 363 sub nom. Roman
Catholic Separate School Trustees for Tiny et al. v. The King,
[1928] 2 W.W.R. 641, and this Court is bound by that
decision.

In the 60 years since the Tiny case, it has been a recognized
and accepted fact of constitutional life in Ontario that
separate school rights under s. 93 do not include any
entitlement to public funding beyond the elementary school
level. On this basis, the province was not required to fund
separate secondary schools. The funding which has been extended
to grades 9 and 10 is not before the Court on this reference.

We do not accept the proposition that any benefit given to
separate schools in Ontario by post-Confederation legislation
enacted after the
Charter
by the province under its s. 93 power
to make laws in relation to education is shielded from scrutiny
under the Charter. Bill 30 does not confer a right or privilege
guaranteed to Roman Catholic separate schools by or under the
Constitution and is not immune from Charter scrutiny. Section
29 only applies to rights and privileges in respect of separate
schools which are constitutionally guaranteed. In Ontario the
rights and privileges under
s. 93(1)
are the only ones which
fall in this category.

Prior to the coming into force of the
Charter
, there is no
doubt that Bill 30 would have been a valid exercise of
provincial legislative authority. However the Charter is part
of Canada's Constitution, our supreme law; it establishes a new
relationship between the individual and the State. Its text
marks the metes and bounds of government authority and
individual autonomy. If Bill 30 is inconsistent with the
Charter, it is the duty of the courts as guardians of our
Constitution, to declare the Bill of no force or effect.

In our opinion, Bill 30 is inconsistent with
s. 15(1)
of the

Charter
which gives to every individual the right to equal
benefit of the law without discrimination based on religion. If
this right is to mean anything, it must mean at least that the
followers of one religion are not to be the beneficiaries of
greater benefits provided by law than the followers of other
religions. Bill 30 provides benefits on the basis of religion
to one religious group only and is therefore in direct conflict
with this right.

Nor has Bill 30 been justified as a reasonable limit under
s.
1
of the
Charter
. Although one can sympathize with Roman
Catholic parents who must pay both public school taxes and
denominational school fees, the same holds true for members of
other religions who send their children to religious schools.
Ontario today is a multicultural and pluralistic society
composed of people of many diverse social, ethnic, racial and
religious backgrounds. Religion is a dominant feature of their
multicultural heritage and, by the very terms of
s. 27
of the
Charter, the multicultural heritage of Canadians is to be
preserved and enhanced. In our opinion, therefore, Bill 30 is
unconstitutional and would be of no force or effect if enacted.

We turn now to a fuller discussion of these conclusions.

II.  HISTORICAL DEVELOPMENT OF THE SCHOOL SYSTEM IN  ONTARIO

It is necessary at the outset to trace the history of the
separate school system in Ontario in order to determine what
rights or privileges Roman Catholics had by law at the time of
Confederation under s. 93(1), and the effect of legislation
subsequently enacted. This has been reviewed to a considerable
extent in the decisions in the Tiny case starting with the
decision of Rose J. at trial (the "trial decision"). His
decision was unanimously affirmed by the Appellate Division of
this Court (the "Appellate decision"). On a further appeal the
six members of the Supreme Court of Canada were equally divided
in their views (the "Supreme Court of Canada decision").
Finally the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council dismissed
an appeal to it from the judgment of the Supreme Court of
Canada (the "Privy Council decision"). The Annual Reports of
the Normal, Model, Grammar, and Common Schools, and the Journal
of Education also throw light on the type of education
provided. Dr. Egerton Ryerson, the author of those reports, had
a great influence on the development of our educational system.
He had been assistant superintendent prior to 1846 and was
chief superintendent of the schools of Upper Canada and later,
Ontario, from that time until 1876.

A  Pre-Confederation development

Prior to Confederation there were three principal classes of
schools: common schools, grammar schools and separate schools.
The establishment of common schools and grammar schools
preceded the establishment of separate schools.

In 1807 provision was made by statute (Public Schools Act,
1807 (U.C.), c. 6) for the establishment of public schools in
every district, for the appointment of trustees to manage them
and for the appropriation of funds annually for teachers. In
1816 the first Common Schools Act, 1816 (U.C.), c. 36, was
passed. The schools were renamed as common schools. While
trustees were given the power and authority to govern the
common schools, they were required to report to a district
board of education as to the books used and the rules and
regulations in effect. The district board in turn could direct
that the books should not be used, or could rescind the rules
and regulations.

By 1840 provision had also been made for the establishment of
grammar schools with their own trustees ["An Act to provide for
the advancement of Education in this Province", 1839 (U.C.), c.
10].

The common and grammar schools appear to have been
undenominational although there was provision for moral and
religious instruction.

The first statutory provision for separate schools was in
1841 (Common Schools Act, 1841 (U.C.), c. 18, s. 11), and it
gave inhabitants professing a religious faith different from
that of the majority the right to have a separate common school
established which would receive its proportion of the moneys
appropriated by law. Such schools were to be subject to the
visitations, conditions, rules and obligations provided for
other common schools. Common school commissioners regulated the
courses of study, the books to be used and the general rules
for the conduct of the schools (s. 7, Fourthly). In other words
there was local autonomy. Provision was, however, made for a
superintendent of education in the province who would make
suggestions for further uniformity in the conduct of the common
schools (s. 4, Fifthly). In 1843, by an Act for the
establishment and maintenance of Common Schools in Upper Canada
(Common Schools Act, 1843 (U.C.), c. 29, s. 55), it was
provided that where a teacher was a Protestant, the Roman
Catholics would be entitled to a separate school with a teacher
of their own religious persuasion. This was the first such
reference to separate schools. A corresponding right was given
to Protestants to have a school with a Protestant teacher,
where the teacher was a Roman Catholic.

These separate common schools were still subject to the
"visitations, conditions, rules and obligations" for other
common schools (s. 56). Authority over common schools became
more centralized with the appointment of a chief superintendent
with power to give instructions for their better organization
and government (s. 6). The power of the local trustees to
regulate courses of study and textbooks was narrowed by a
requirement that it was subject to approval by the township,
town or city superintendent (s. 46, No. 7).

The Common Schools Act of 1843 was replaced in 1846 by
another Act (Common Schools Act, 1846 (U.C.), c. 20), which
further reduced the powers of local trustees over common school
education. It took away their authority to prescribe courses of
study or the books to be used. A board of education was
established. It had the power to recommend or disapprove of
books, and to aid the superintendent of schools with its
counsel and advice.

With the Upper Canada School Act, 1850 (U.C.), c. 48, the
local autonomy which had been eroded by the legislation in 1843
and 1846 was replaced by a central authority called the Council
for Public Instruction of Upper Canada, comprising not more
than nine persons of whom the chief superintendent was to be
one (s. 36). It was given broad powers to make such regulations
from time to time, as it deemed expedient, for the
organization, government and discipline of common schools and
for the classification of schools and teachers, and for school
libraries. It also had power to recommend or disapprove of the
use of textbooks. No grant was to be applied in aid of a school
which used a book which had been disapproved (s. 38). This Act
authorized the appointment of a chief superintendent of schools
for Upper Canada (s. 34), one of whose duties was to apportion
annually all moneys granted or provided by the Legislature for
the support of common schools in Upper Canada, and not
otherwise appropriated by the Act, to the several counties,
townships, cities, towns and incorporated villages on the basis
of population (s. 35).

Regulations under this Act were issued in 1850 so that there
would be only one series of textbooks in a school. Rose J. in
the Tiny case, trial decision at pp. 109-10, stated:

The books appear to be quite elementary; and the "programme
of the examination and classification of teachers" prescribed
by the Council of Public Instruction is one that could not
have been prescribed if the common schools had been equipped
for anything beyond the imparting of elementary education (p.
101 of the manual issued in 1850).

Provision was also made for the establishment of separate
schools for Protestants, Roman Catholics or coloured people to
be under the same regulations as common schools generally, and
to be entitled to share in the school fund based on the
proportion of the average attendance in such schools to the
average attendance in all common schools in the municipality
(s. 19). Trustees of school sections in rural areas were to
permit all residents between the ages of 5 and 21 to attend a
common school (except the children of persons for whom a
separate school had been established) (s. 12, Thirteenthly).
Urban trustees did not have such an explicit duty. Their local
superintendents had to report students in two groups: those
between the ages of 5 and 16 years; and those between the ages
of 16 and 21 years (s. 31, Tenthly, 2nd).

While grammar schools had been established long before, the
Grammar School Act, 1853 (U.C.), c. 186, was intended to cause
grammar schools to take their place as intermediate schools
between the common schools and the university. They were to
teach in:

5. ... all the higher branches of a practical English and
Commercial Education including the Elements of Natural
Philosophy and Mechanics, and also in the Latin and Greek
Languages and Mathematics so far as to prepare students for
University College or any College affiliated to the
University of Toronto ...

The Council of Public Instruction prescribed the list of
textbooks, the programme of studies and the general rules and
regulations (s. 6). In his 1850 Report, Dr. Egerton Ryerson, as
Chief Superintendent, stated at p. 22:

The Grammar School should be a connecting link between the
Common Schools and the University; the Common Schools should
be feeders of the Grammar Schools as these should be the
feeders of the University.

The Upper Canada Supplementary School Act, 1853 (U.C.), c.
185, provided for separate schools to share in the legislative
common school grant and for persons sending their children to
separate schools to be exempted from rates imposed for common
schools where they had contributed an equal amount to the
separate schools (s. 4).

The laws relating to separate schools in Upper Canada were
amended in 1855 by the Separate Schools Act, 1855 (U.C.), c.
131, better known as the Tache Act. It gave the trustees power
to levy school rates on those sending children to or supporting
the separate schools, but the trustees had to perform the
duties required of trustees of common schools (s. 8). It
provided for the exemption of separate school supporters from
paying rates imposed for the support of common schools (s. 12).
It also gave separate schools the right to share in the fund
annually granted by the Legislature for the support of common
schools in the proportion that the number of children attending
them bore to the average number of school pupils in the
municipality (s. 13).

Common schools had three divisions and six prescribed
classes. The regulations for common schools published by the
Council of Public Instruction in 1858 prescribed the order and
classification of studies with definite rules as to what was to
be studied in each of the three divisions of the school. As
Rose J. stated in the Tiny case, trial decision at p. 122:

In the third or higher division the work was a little in
advance of what would be called elementary -- for instance,
the first six books of Euclid were to be studied, and
subjects such as trigonometry and the elements of geology
might be taken up at the discretion of the school
authorities.

While children between the ages of 5 and 21 were to be
permitted to attend common schools, including separate schools,
some older students were given more advanced teaching that
would fit them to enter university even though it was not
prescribed.

The legislation governing common schools at the time of
Confederation was the Common Schools Act, C.S.U.C. 1859, c. 64.
It contained similar provisions to those referred to in the
Upper Canada School Act of 1850 and largely consolidated the
statutory provisions respecting common schools.

The Separate Schools Act, C.S.U.C. 1859, c. 65, made the main
provisions of the Common Schools Act of 1859 applicable to
separate schools, and provided that the trustees of each
separate school should perform the same duties and be subject
to the same penalties as trustees of common schools.

The legislation which governed separate schools at the time
of Confederation was the Separate Schools Act, 1863 (U.C.), c.
5. It was known as the Scott Act. It was an Act to restore to
Roman Catholics in Upper Canada certain rights which they
formerly enjoyed in respect of separate schools and to bring
the provisions of the law respecting separate schools into
harmony with the provisions of the law respecting common
schools. It authorized Roman Catholics to establish separate
schools and to elect trustees (ss. 2-6). The trustees were
empowered to levy school rates upon persons sending children to
or subscribing towards the support of such schools and they
were given:

7. ... all the powers in respect of Separate Schools, that
the Trustees of common Schools have and possess under the
provisions of the Act relating to Common Schools.

Under s. 14, the supporters of separate schools were to be
exempted from the payment of common school rates upon giving
the required notice. As to the annual legislative grant, s. 20
provided:

20. Every Separate School shall be entitled to a share in
the fund annually granted by the Legislature of this Province
for the support of Common Schools, and shall be entitled also
to a share in all other public grants, investments and
allotments for Common School purposes now made or hereafter
to be made by the Province or the Municipal authorities,
according to the average number of pupils attending such
school during the twelve next preceding months, or during the
number of months which may have elapsed from the
establishment of a new Separate School, as compared with the
whole average number of pupils attending school in the same
City, Town, Village or Township.

The Scott Act thus expanded the funding of separate schools so
that they would be on the same basis as common schools. The
centralized nature of the school system was confirmed by s. 26,
which made the separate schools subject to inspection by the
chief superintendent, and also to such regulations as might be
passed from time to time by the Council of Public Instruction
of Upper Canada.

The Separate School Manual of 1863 set out in app. "H" the
courses of instruction to be completed in Catholic separate
schools in the First, Second and Third Divisions as adopted by
the Council of Public Instruction. It referred to five extra
subjects for boys and an equal number for girls which could be
taken at the discretion of the school authorities, but no two,
however, during the same term.

In 1866, unsuccessful attempts were made by both Upper
Canadian Catholics (the Bell Bill) and Lower Canadian
Protestants (the Langevin Bill) to have legislation passed
which would give them even greater privileges although the
existing privileges of the Protestants in Lower Canada were
said to be greater than those enjoyed by the Catholics in Upper
Canada. On August 7, 1866, the Attorney-General, John A.
Macdonald, announced to the Legislative Assembly that both the
Upper Canadian and the Lower Canadian school bills had been
dropped.

B
Section 93
of the
Constitution Act, 1867

Section 93
of the
Constitution Act, 1867
represented a
compromise. Its wording was carefully chosen. The resolution
adopted at the Quebec Conference on October 10, 1864, contained
the following provision respecting education:

The Local Legislatures shall have power to make Laws
respecting the following subjects:

. . . . .

6. Education: saving the rights and privileges which the
Protestant or Catholic minority in both Canadas may possess
as to their Denominational Schools, at the time when the
Union goes into operation.

(Browne, Documents on the Confederation of British North
America (1969, at pp. 160-1.) In the first draft of the British
North America Act, February 9, 1867, the wording was changed to
read "any Right or Privilege with respect to Denominational
Schools which any Class of Persons have by Law".

Section 93
of the
Constitution Act, 1867
as enacted provides
as follows:

93. In and for each Province the Legislature may
exclusively make Laws in relation to Education, subject and
according to the following Provisions:--

(
1
) Nothing in any such Law shall prejudicially affect any
Right or Privilege with respect to Denominational Schools
which any Class of Persons have by Law in the Province at the
Union:

(
2
) All the Powers, Privileges, and Duties at the Union by
Law conferred and imposed in Upper Canada on the Separate
Schools and School Trustees of the Queen's Roman Catholic
Subjects shall be and the same are hereby extended to the
Dissentient Schools of the Queen's Protestant and Roman
Catholic Subjects in Quebec:

(
3
) Where in any Province a System of Separate or
Dissentient Schools exists by Law at the Union or is
thereafter established by the Legislature of the Province, an
Appeal shall lie to the Governor General in Council from any
Act or Decision of any Provincial Authority affecting any
Right or Privilege of the Protestant or Roman Catholic
Minority of the Queen's Subjects in relation to Education:

(
4
) In case any such Provincial Law as from Time to Time
seems to the Governor General in Council requisite for the
due Execution of the Provisions of this Section is not made,
or in case any Decision of the Governor General in Council on

any Decision of the Governor General in Council under this

Before turning to consider the rights and privileges as to the
funding of separate schools guaranteed to Roman Catholics in
Ontario under
s. 93(1)
, it is necessary to review the post-
Confederation history of the school system.

C  Post-Confederation history

In 1871 important changes were made in the system of common
and grammar schools by "An Act to Improve the Common and
Grammar Schools of the Province of Ontario", 1871 (Ont.), c.
33. Common schools were to be designated as public schools (s.
1) and were to provide free education to children from 7 to 12
years of age (s. 3). Grammar schools were to be known as high
schools in which provision was to be made for the teaching of
"the higher branches of an English and commercial education,
including the natural sciences, with special reference to
agriculture, and, also, the Latin, Greek, French and German
languages" (s. 34).

Under the Programme of Course of Study for Public Schools,
1871, pupils could pass an entrance examination on the subjects
of the first classes of the public school (equivalent to grades
1 to 8), or they could complete the whole programme of studies
in the public school. The 1871 Act and regulations did not in
any way affect the separate schools.

Regulations for the government of high schools which were put
into operation in 1873 give the general impression that the
standard set was considerably higher than that set for the
advanced divisions of the common schools and separate schools
in 1863. The work in the lower forms of the high schools seems
to have been no more advanced than that prescribed for the
upper forms of the former common (and separate) schools: Rose
J. in Tiny case, trial decision at p. 127.

The Consolidated Public School Act, 1874 (Ont.), c. 28, s.
26, restored the obligation of rural school trustees to admit
all residents between the ages of 5 and 21 to attend the school
(except children of persons for whom a separate school had
been established).

In 1896 the concept of continuation classes with higher
grants was introduced. The Public Schools Act, 1896 (Ont.), c.
70, provided that where there was no high school then a public
school could provide continuation classes (s. 8). No levy of
rates for public school purposes was to apply to supporters of
Roman Catholic separate schools (s. 4).

In 1899 the concept of continuation classes with higher
funding was extended to separate schools. "An Act to Improve
the Laws respecting Public Schools, 1899" (Ont.), c. 36, s. 1,
empowered the school corporation where there was no high school
to establish in the public or separate school over which it had
jurisdiction such courses of study in addition to those
provided for the fifth form (grades 9 and 10) of public school
as may be approved by the regulations of the Education
Department. These classes were to be known as continuation
classes. The trustees of both public and separate schools were
to have the same right to levy rates for the tuition of pupils
attending continuation classes as they had under the Public
Schools Act, 1896 or the Separate Schools Act, 1886 (Ont.), c.
46, for pupils under their immediate jurisdiction.

In 1899 "An Act to amend the Separate Schools Act", 1899
(Ont.), c. 37, provided for the establishment of a separate
school board in a portion of the province not surveyed into
townships, even though there might not be a public school
board.

Finally in 1908, legislation was passed dividing continuation
classes into fifth classes and continuation schools (offering
fifth and sixth classes). Fifth class comprised what is now
grades 9 and 10, and sixth class comprised what is now grades
11 and 12. By "An Act respecting Separate Schools Fifth Classes
and Continuation Schools", 1908 (Ont.), c. 68, subject to the
regulations of the Department of Education, the separate school
boards were given the same powers, duties and obligations as
public school corporations where there was no high school as to
the establishment and maintenance of continuation schools and
fifth classes (s. 2).

The Deputy Minister of Education, Dr. A. H. U. Colquhoun,
realizing that sixth classes operated in some separate schools,
refused to allow separate school boards to use taxes for
classes after the fifth class. In October, 1915, he told them
that they could not do work beyond the fifth class: affidavit
of Robert Thomas Dixon, sworn September 4, 1985, para. 82. In
the result, separate school boards could provide continuation
classes and fifth classes where there were no high schools, but
could not establish their own high schools or share in the
legislative grants for high schools. For grant purposes, grades
9 and 10 in the separate school system appear to have been
treated as elementary grades. Although they were exempt from
the taxes levied for public schools giving elementary
education, separate school supporters were not exempt from the
taxes levied for public high schools.

The Tiny case

In deciding whether Roman Catholics had any right or
privilege by law to the funding of secondary school education
in separate schools within
s. 93(1)
of the
Constitution Act,
1867
, the Tiny case is the key decision.

The proceedings came before the Supreme Court of Ontario by a
petition of right brought by the Roman Catholic separate school
trustees for school section No. 2 in the Township of Tiny on
behalf of themselves and all other boards of trustees of Roman
Catholic separate schools in Ontario. The suppliants claimed:

(1) a declaration that certain sections of certain Acts passed
by the Legislature of Ontario, in so far as they prejudicially
affected rights in respect to denominational schools secured to
Roman Catholics by
s. 93(1)
, were beyond the powers of the
Legislature and were invalid;

(2) the right to establish and conduct courses of study and
grades of education such as were conducted in continuation
schools, collegiate institutes and high schools;

(3) that Roman Catholic separate school supporters were exempt
from rates for the support of such schools which were not
conducted by their boards of trustees;

(4) that separate schools were entitled under the Separate
Schools Act of 1863 to share on the basis therein provided in
all legislative grants for the support of common schools
including all grants for the support of secondary schools, and
that legislation enacted since Confederation altering the basis
of distribution for separate schools prejudicially affected
their rights under
s. 93(1)
and was ultra vires;

(
5
) judgment for the difference between the amount paid to them
and the amount to which they would have been entitled under the
Separate Schools Act of 1863.

The issue in the Tiny case was not as to the right of Roman
Catholic separate schools to give elementary education and
receive funding therefor, but as to their right to give
secondary education in continuation schools, collegiate
institutes and high schools and to receive the necessary
funding.

Rose J. in his trial judgment on May 13, 1926, traced in
great detail the legislative changes in the school system. He
concluded that the statutes and regulations impeached did not
prejudicially affect any right or privilege with respect to
denominational schools which the class of persons represented
by the suppliants had by law in Upper Canada at Confederation.
As he stated at p. 138:

... the right or privilege that the British North America Act
preserves was a right or privilege that the law gave and that
could have been exercised even in the face of opposition.

And at p. 140:

... the trustees of the separate schools would have been
bound to obey any regulation which the Council of Public
Instruction for Upper Canada had seen fit to pass with the
object of fixing the point of commencement of the grammar-
school course and the point beyond which the education of
pupils in the common schools should not proceed.

As school corporations they had the corporate capacity to teach
what might properly be taught in "common" schools, that is,
what might properly be taught in the primary schools in Upper
Canada. The fact that some of the common schools did work which
was really the work of secondary schools was not determinative
of the matter. If the Council of Public Instruction had
attempted to encroach upon the normal statutory role of common
schools to give elementary education, then an appeal against
such an unfair exercise of its provincial power could have been
made under
s. 93(3)
of the
Constitution Act, 1867
. The
obligation on rural common school trustees to permit persons
between the ages of 5 and 21 to attend their schools and the
right of urban common school trustees to do so did not mean
that the trustees had an obligation to provide tuition suitable
for all persons within that range.

The judgment of Rose J. was affirmed by the five judges of
the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Ontario.

On a further appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada the
Appellate decision was affirmed, there being an equal division
of opinion in the Supreme Court of Canada. Anglin C.J.C. and
Rinfret J. would have allowed the appeal on all grounds.
Mignault J. was in agreement except as to legislative grants;
he considered that the Separate Schools Act of 1863 did not
apply to special grants or to grants for particular purposes.
Anglin C.J.C. felt that it was clear that in 1867 the trustees
of separate schools had the right by law to provide in such
schools the secondary education requisite to enable the
children of their supporters to matriculate into the
university, to enter the normal school, and to take up the
study of any of the "learned professions". At p. 667 S.C.R.,
pp. 870-1 D.L.R., he stated:

While our attention was not drawn to any explicit evidence
to that effect, there is little room for doubt that the
attendance of pupils at the common schools who were taking
the courses of high school work was included in the returns
made for the purpose of ascertaining the proportion of the
legislative grants to which the several school sections in
which such schools were carried on were entitled ... and also
in determining the amount of public moneys to be apportioned
to the separate schools ... That could properly be done only
if the trustees of common schools had the legal right to
conduct the classes in which high school or classical
education was given.

Duff, Newcombe and Lamont JJ. were of the opinion that the
appeal should be dismissed. Duff J. stated at pp. 701-2 S.C.R.,
p. 901 D.L.R.:

The programmes of study promulgated by the Council are in
evidence, so, also, are the regulations prescribing the
qualifications of teachers. The programmes are not framed
with the view of fitting pupils for the university, as at
once appears from a comparison of the list of subjects taught
with requirements for matriculation; the qualifications for
teachers are just as plainly not designed to provide
instruction for any but the most elementary schools ...

. . . . .

... it is beyond doubt that the school books necessary for
effective instruction of pupils reading for matriculation in
the university or for entrance into the learned professions,
could not, if the law were observed, be used in common
schools, at any time after 1847, when the first list of
recommended books was sanctioned ...

Finally there was an appeal to the Judicial Committee of the
Privy Council,
1928 CanLII 355 (UK JCPC)
, [1928] 3 D.L.R. 753, [1928] A.C. 363, [1928] 2
W.W.R. 641, which was dismissed.

As Viscount Haldane said at p. 764 D.L.R., p. 378 A.C. of the
Privy Council decision:

It is plain that the policy laid down from the commencement
of the nineteenth century up to 1855 was to place all the
common schools, including the separate schools, which were
merely a special form of these, under ultimate state
regulation.

At p. 769 D.L.R., pp. 385-6 A.C. he further stated:

The provincial legislature is supreme in matters of
education, excepting so far as s. 93 of the B.N.A. Act
restricts its authority. Subsection 1 preserves as they stood
any rights and the privileges given in relation to
denominational schools by law in 1867. The question,
therefore, is whether the Province could then as the law
stood so control the courses of study and the general range
and quality of the text books used, as to enable the
educational authorities of the Province to prescribe the
graduation of the separate school and the stages in which
instruction should be given in it. Examination of the
statutes and of the history of the subject have satisfied
their Lordships that, while a settlement was come to in 1863
with both Roman Catholics and Protestants, a settlement which
in so far as it remained unaltered at Confederation, must be
strictly maintained, the Province showed in the wording of
the successive earlier statutes the intention to preserve for
the rest the power to mould the educational system in the
interests of the public at large, as distinguished from any
section of it, however important.

The Judicial Committee did not consider that separate school
trustees could give secondary education in their schools
otherwise than by the express or implied permission of the
Council of Public Instruction. At p. 771 D.L.R., p. 387 A.C.,
Viscount Haldane stated:

The separate school was only a special form of common school,
and the council could in the case of each determine the
courses to be pursued and the extent of the education to be
imparted. A full power of regulation, such as the purpose of
the statutes quoted renders appropriate, is what suggests
itself, and this is the natural outcome of a scheme which
never appears to have really varied. Such expressions as
"organization," "government," "discipline" and
"classification," do, in their Lordships' interpretation
of them, imply a real control of the separate schools.

The Judicial Committee concluded that it was not ultra vires
upon Confederation to make new appropriations even though the
amount which would otherwise have come to the separate schools
would be diminished. The power to regulate did not include the
power to abolish. The province could not validly enact
legislation that would threaten the existence of separate
schools. There was no basis for concluding, however, that the
regulations under consideration in the appeal went that far.
They were regulations relating to education and did not
interfere with the denominational character of separate schools
and so were within the proper ambit of provincial regulation.

If separate school trustees could not offer secondary
education as a matter of right, there was no obligation on the
province to fund separate schools beyond the level of
elementary education. Government funding at a higher level was
accordingly a matter of government policy rather than being
based on constitutional right.

Historical developments since the Tiny case

Between 1945 and 1950 a comprehensive inquiry was made into
the system of education in Ontario by a Royal Commission on
Education under the chairmanship of Mr. Justice John A. Hope.
The majority report concluded that at Confederation Roman
Catholics had the right to operate a separate form of common
(elementary) schools but had no similar right with respect
to secondary schools. It recommended that the existing eight
years of elementary education and five years of secondary
education be changed to six years elementary, four years
intermediate and three years senior. Separate schools were to
be permitted for only the first six elementary grades. The
minority report concluded that separate schools had long
enjoyed the right to provide a programme from kindergarten to
the end of grade 10. The majority report was never implemented.

In October, 1962, the Roman Catholic bishops presented a
brief to Premier Robarts calling for the same advantages,
rights and opportunity to grow as their secular counterparts.
More particularly, they asked for an increased share of
corporation taxes together with full funding to the end of
grade 13.

Premier Robarts, however, did not favour the extension of
provincial grants to separate schools beyond grade 10. He
stated in the Legislature of Ontario Debates on February 21,
1963, at p. 922:

Such a course as has been suggested would constitute a
complete reversal of policies followed by governments under
all political parties for the past hundred years.

The Government of Ontario in turn, through the Ontario Tax
Foundation Plan of 1964, substantially increased provincial
grants to separate schools, particularly equalization grants to
compensate separate schools which received less from local
property tax than public schools.

In 1967, the Ontario Committee on Taxation recommended that
the revenue derived from local property taxes paid by
corporations should be equalized so that all schools in the
Ontario system would receive the same fiscal treatment.

In 1968, the Hall-Dennis Report stated:

In the implementation of the proposed plan for larger units
of administration for education in Ontario, announced by
Prime Minister Robarts on November 14, 1967, some arrangement
acceptable to all should be found -- one which will bring the
two tax-supported systems into administrative co-operation,
preserving what is considered by the separate school
supporters as essential to their system, and at the same time
making possible a great deal of co-operation and sharing of
special services, avoiding duplication in many areas and
services, with a consequent saving of tax dollars; but of
infinitely greater significance, an arrangement which will
bring to an end a controversy that has burdened the
administration of education in Ontario since Confederation.

In the following year, the Ontario Separate School Trustees'
Association brief on Equal Opportunity for Continuous Education
in Separate Schools in Ontario advocated the extension of the
Roman Catholic separate school system to grade 13 and the
provision of full funding.

On June 1, 1970, the Ecumenical Study Commission which
comprised members of both the principal Protestant
denominations and the Roman Catholic Church supported the basic
position of the above brief.

In 1970, the Ontario Liberal Caucus supported the extension
of education in separate schools to the end of secondary
education. The New Democratic Party in turn called for full
grants for Catholic school children to grade 13 on condition
that separate school boards and public school boards join in
planning shared facilities and services to meet the needs of
all students in every community.

On August 31, 1971, Premier Davis announced that the
government would not extend funding to separate schools beyond
grade 10 for the following reasons:

If, on the other hand, the Government of Ontario were
arbitrarily to decide to establish and maintain, out of
public funds, a complete educational system determined by
denominational and religious considerations, such a decision
would fragment the present system beyond recognition and
repair, and do so to the disadvantage of all those who have
come to want for their children a public school system free
of a denominational or sectarian character.

. . . . .

To embark upon such a policy could not be, in reason or
justice, limited to some faiths and denied to others.

Before 1978, provincial legislative grants for grades 9 and
10 of separate schools were made at the elementary school level
rather than at the secondary school level which was higher.
Commencing in 1978 such grants were increased to 90% of the
secondary school level: Robert M. Stamp, "The Historical
Background to Separate Schools in Ontario", June, 1985.

On June 12, 1984, Premier Davis announced that the government
had decided to provide full funding for all secondary grades in
Roman Catholic separate schools: Hansard No. 69, June 12, 1984,
pp. 2414-7.

On July 26, 1984, by Order in Council, O.C. 2049/84, a
Commission on Private Schools in Ontario was established with
Dr. Bernard Shapiro as the sole commissioner. Part of its
responsibility was to consider the relation of private schools
to publicly supported school boards and whether funding should
be extended to such independent schools. Since the hearing of
this reference, Dr. Shapiro has released his report.

Both opposition parties have confirmed their support of the
government's policy announcement of June 12, 1984.

D  Bill 30

On July 4, 1985, after a change of government, the Honourable
Sean Conway, Minister of Education, introduced Bill 30, the
Education Amendment Act, 1985, in the Legislature to extend
full public funding to Roman Catholic secondary schools. We
turn now to consider the provisions of the Bill.

Election to perform duties of secondary school board

The Bill establishes a system whereby a separate school board
can elect by by-law approved by the Minister to perform the
duties of a secondary school board. The Minister's approval is
to be given only after the Planning and Implementation
Commission has concluded that the first annual implementation
plan will permit the separate school board to provide secondary
school education and will promote the best interests of public
education in Ontario (s. 136a).

Funding

When an election has been made and approved by the Minister,
the separate school board becomes a "Roman Catholic school
board" and is entitled to share in the legislative grants for
secondary school purposes (s. 136e). In the first year the
funding is provided for grades 9 and 10 for the boards that
were not previously providing grades 9 and 10, and for grades
9, 10 and 11 for the boards that were previously providing
grades 9 and 10. In subsequent years funding is extended by one
further grade each year until all secondary school grades are
covered (s. 136g). Section 136f provides that, where, "before
the coming into force of this Act," the Planning and
Implementation Commission favourably reports to the Minister
with respect to the implementation plan of a separate school
board, the board becomes entitled to funding as of the first
day of the school year commencing in 1985.

Taxes

Separate school supporters within the jurisdiction of a Roman
Catholic school board are exempt from payment of rates or taxes
for secondary school purposes of a public board (s. 136j). On
the other hand they are liable for rates or taxes for the
support of Roman Catholic separate schools. The provisions of
the Education Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 129, for the levying and
collection of the rates or taxes for separate school purposes
are extended to secondary school purposes in respect of a Roman
Catholic school board (s. 136k).

Teachers

Every public board of education (which is defined to include
both a board of education or a secondary school board
established under s. 69), is required by s. 136l to prepare a
designated list of both its teachers and non-teaching staff
whose services will not be required because of the election of
a Roman Catholic school board to perform the duties of a
secondary school board. For a period of ten years following its
election, the Roman Catholic school board is required to fill
positions on its teaching staff by offering employment to
persons on the designated list who have the necessary
qualifications. These persons have the right to the annual rate
of salary and the seniority and probationary or permanent
status that they would have had if they had continued with the
public board. In the same way, non-teaching staff openings have
to be offered to persons on the designated list in
substantially similar positions.

Pupils

A pupil who is qualified to attend a public secondary school
operated by a public board is entitled to attend a secondary
school operated by a Roman Catholic school board, if the public
secondary school is in the area of jurisdiction of the Roman
Catholic school board, and if the director of education or
other appropriate official certifies that there is
accommodation available. A pupil qualified to attend a
secondary school operated by a Roman Catholic school board has
a similar right to attend a secondary school operated by a
public board on the same terms.

A pupil who so attends a Roman Catholic separate school, but
who is not a Roman Catholic, is not exempt from religious
instruction unless a written application is made and either:

(a) the pupil is enrolled in a programme that is not otherwise
available in the secondary school operated by the public board,
or

(b) it is impractical for the pupil to attend the secondary
school operated by the public board by reason of distance or
physical or mental handicaps (s. 136o).

Transfer of property

Section 136x empowers the Planning and Implementation
Commission to resolve disputes between a public board and a
Roman Catholic school board in respect of a number of matters
that, by virtue of other sections, are the subject of
negotiations. The Commission appoints a tribunal which is
authorized, inter alia, to transfer the use or ownership of
real or personal property, or both, from the public board to
the Roman Catholic school board.

III  THE PROPER INTERPRETATION OF S. 93 OF THE CONSTITUTION
ACT, 1867

It is necessary now to consider the interpretation to be
given to
s. 93
of the
Constitution Act, 1867
. For convenience
we will repeat the wording of the section:

93. In and for each Province the Legislature may
exclusively make Laws in relation to Education, subject and
according to the following Provisions:--

(1) Nothing in any such Law shall prejudicially affect any
Right or Privilege with respect to Denominational Schools
which any Class of Persons have by law in the Province at the
Union:

(2) All the Powers, Privileges, and Duties at the Union by
Law conferred and imposed in Upper Canada on the Separate
Schools and School Trustees of the Queen's Roman Catholic
Subjects shall be and the same are hereby extended to the
Dissentient Schools of the Queen's Protestant and Roman
Catholic Subjects in Quebec:

(3) Where in any Province a System of Separate or
Dissentient Schools exists by Law at the union or is
thereafter established by the Legislature of the Province, an
Appeal shall lie to the Governor General in Council from any
Act or Decision of any Provincial Authority affecting any
Right or Privilege of the Protestant or Roman Catholic
Minority of the Queen's Subjects in relation to Education:

(4) In case any such Provincial Law as from Time to Time
seems to the Governor General in Council requisite for the
due Execution of the Provisions of this Section is not made,
or in case any Decision of the Governor General in Council on
any Appeal under this Section is not duly executed by the
proper Provincial Authority in that Behalf, then and in every
such Case, and as far only as the Circumstances of each Case
require, the Parliament of Canada may make remedial Laws for
the due Execution of the Provisions of this Section and of
any Decision of the Governor General in Council under this
Section.

The powers of the provincial Legislatures in relation to
education under
s. 93
are broad. They may exclusively make laws
in relation to education subject to s-ss.(1), (2), (3) and (4).

Section 93(1)
is the provision most relevant to this reference.
In order to claim its protection the following conditions must
be met:

"(a) there must be a right or privilege affecting a
denominational school;

"(b) enjoyed by a particular class of persons;

"(c) by law;

"(d) in effect at the time of the Union;

"(e) and which is prejudicially affected."

A.-G. Que. v. Greater Hull School Board et al.,
1984 CanLII 29 (SCC)
, [1984] 2 S.C.R.
575 at p. 582, 15 D.L.R. (4th) 651 at p. 657, 28 M.P.L.R. 146,
per Chouinard J.

We will deal with the interpretation of each of these
conditions in turn. Firstly, s. 93(1) is limited to a right or
privilege with respect to denominational schools. Roman
Catholic separate schools are clearly denominational schools.
It will be noted that
s. 93(3)
is broader than s. 93(1) because
it refers to rights or privileges in relation to education, and
not just rights or privileges in relation to denominational
schools.

Secondly, in Ottawa Separate School Trustees v. Mackell
(1916),
1916 CanLII 418 (UK JCPC)
, 32 D.L.R. 1 at p. 4, [1917] A.C. 62 at p. 69, the
Judicial Committee decided that the "class of persons" to whom
the right or privilege is reserved must be determined according
to religious belief, and not according to race or language. It
concluded that, in relation to denominational teaching, Roman
Catholics together formed within the meaning of the section a
class of persons. That class cannot be subdivided into other
classes by considerations of the language of the people by whom
that faith is held. In Mackell it was held that s. 93(1)
protected the power of the trustees to determine "the kind and
description" of schools, but it did not extend to determining
whether English or French should be the language of instruction
in the schools. This came within the Legislature's general
power in relation to education but was not a right or privilege
with respect to denominational schools within s. 93(1).

As this Court stated in Reference re Education Act of Ontario
and Minority Language Education Rights (1984),
1984 CanLII 1832 (ON CA)
, 47 O.R. (2d) 1
at p. 48, 10 D.L.R. (4th) 491 at pp. 537-8, 27 M.P.L.R. 1 (the
"Minority Language Reference"):

The Tiny Township case, to which we adverted earlier,
decided that the province enjoys "a full power of regulation"
with respect to the operation of denominational schools and
may regulate them without violating the terms of
s. 93
. So
long as the legislation regulates education and does not
threaten the existence of the separate schools or interfere
with their denominational character it is valid. The Privy
Council in this case ruled in favour of a provincial law
prohibiting separate schools in Ontario from offering
secondary education beyond grade 10, and reducing the
separate schools' share of the public funds appropriated for
education. On its analysis of the impugned legislation and
the historical background, the rights and privileges in issue
related to education and not denomination and were therefore
a legitimate subject of provincial regulation.

However, legislation withdrawing indefinitely the right of
elected trustees to manage separate schools contravenes s.
93(1). This was the situation in Ottawa Separate School
Trustees v. City of Ottawa (1916),
1916 CanLII 419 (UK JCPC)
, 32 D.L.R. 10, [1917] A.C.
76, a case which arose out of the province's effort to
enforce Reg. 17, the English-language requirement upheld in
Mackell. The Privy Council here invalidated a statute
authorizing the province to withdraw from separate school
trustees all powers over the schools and vest them in a
provincially appointed commission. The statute authorizing
the commission prejudically affected a right to management of
separate schools which formed part of the law of Ontario at
the time of Confederation, and was therefore held ultra
vires.

Similarly, in Hirsch v. Protestant Board School Com'rs of
Montreal [
1928 CanLII 500 (UK JCPC)
, [1928] 1 D.L.R. 1041, [1928] A.C. 200], legislation
which diminished the exclusively denominational character of
separate schools or their management was found invalid. In
that case, the Privy Council struck down a Quebec statute
which prejudicially affected the pre-Confederation right of
the Protestant minority to establish its own schools under
the exclusive management of Protestant trustees for the
exclusive use of Protestant children. The right to establish
and support denominational schools managed by their own
elected trustees is fundamental to the existence of the
separate school system.

With respect to the third condition, with reference to the
words "by law", it seems to have been clearly determined that
only statutory rights or privileges are protected by s. 93(1)
and not those based on long-standing practice or custom. In the
Minority Language Reference this Court said at pp. 45-6 O.R.,
p. 535 D.L.R.:

The constitutionally protected rights or privileges are, by
the terms of s. 93(1), those which "any class of persons" had
"by law" at Confederation. The phrase "by law" [in s.
93(1)] has been construed to mean that only statutory rights
or privileges in existence in 1867 are afforded protection;
long-standing practices, customs or privileges of a voluntary
character do not qualify under s. 93(1); Maher v. Town of
Portland (1874), Wheeler's Confederation Law of Canada 338 at
p. 367; Hirsch v. Protestant Board School Com'rs of Montreal
et al., supra, at p. 1048 D.L.R., p. 210 A.C.

Mulock C.J.O. expressed a similar opinion in the Tiny case,
Appellate decision, at p. 18 O.L.R., p. 914 D.L.R., namely
that:

... the rights and privileges enjoyed by Roman Catholic
separate schools within the meaning of
sec. 93
, provision 1,
are limited to those expressly conferred by the Legislature
of the late Province of Canada and in force at the Union.

See also Ottawa Separate Schools Trustees v. Mackell, supra, at
pp. 2-3 D.L.R., p. 69 A.C.

The fourth condition makes it clear that under s. 93(1), the
only rights and privileges of separate school supporters which
are guaranteed are those which are protected by law at the time
of the Union. It is therefore necessary to see what laws were
in effect in a particular province at that time. It is
interesting to contrast the wording in s. 93(1) with that in
the corresponding provision of s. 22(1) of the Manitoba Act,
1870 (Can.), c. 3, confirmed by the British North America Act,
1871 [renamed Constitution Act, 1871, by the
Constitution Act,
1982, s. 53(1)
, Schedule, item 5]. It provided:

22. In and for the Province, the said Legislature may
exclusively make Laws in relation to Education, subject and
according to the following provisions:--

(1) Nothing in any such Law shall prejudicially affect any
right or privilege with respect to Denominational Schools
which any class of persons have by Law or practice in the
Province at the Union:

(Emphasis added.) In 1870 no denominational rights existed in
law in Manitoba and the words "in practice" were deliberately
added. There existed denominational schools, some of which were
regulated and controlled by the Roman Catholic Church and
others by various Protestant denominations. The Roman Catholics
supported their own schools and did not contribute to the
support of any other schools. In 1871, a law was passed
establishing a system of denominational education. In 1890,
this denominational system was swept away and all ratepayers
had to support the public school system. Roman Catholics and
those of other denominations were still free to establish and
maintain their own schools.

Lord Macnaghten in delivering the judgment of the Judicial
Committee of the Privy Council in City of Winnipeg v. Barrett,

[1892] A.C. 445, stated at p. 453
with reference to s.
22(1):

Evidently the word "practice" is not to be construed as
equivalent to "custom having the force of law". Their
Lordships are convinced that it must have been the intention
of the legislature to preserve every legal right or
privilege, and every benefit or advantage in the nature of a
right or privilege, with respect to denominational schools,
which any class of persons practically enjoyed at the time of
the Union.

The Judicial Committee, however, concluded that there were no
rights or privileges with respect to denominational schools
existing by law or in practice in the province at the Union and
no such rights or privileges had been prejudicially affected by
the Act of 1890. The separate school supporters appealed to the
Governor-General in Council under s. 22(2) which was similar to

s. 93(3)
. Their right to do so was challenged in Re Certain
Statutes of the Province of Manitoba Relating to Education
(1894),
1894 CanLII 80 (SCC)
, 22 S.C.R. 577, on the ground that the Act of 1890
did not "affect" any right or privilege protected by law or
practice at the Union. The Judicial Committee of the Privy
Council reversed the conclusion of the Supreme Court of Canada
on a reference submitted to it, and decided (
[1895] A.C. 202

sub nom. Brophy et al. v. A.-G. Man.) that in view of the levy
made on the Roman Catholic minority for school purposes, it
could not be said that their rights and privileges under s.
22(1) were not prejudicially affected. Section 22(2) was not
limited to rights or privileges protected by law or practice at
the union, and accordingly there was an appeal to the Governor-
General in Council.

In Ontario the rights of separate school supporters which are
constitutionally guaranteed under s. 93(1) are those which
existed by law at the time of the Union on July 1, 1867. It
would seem to be clearly established that both common school
supporters and Roman Catholic separate school supporters were
entitled to the public funding of elementary school education
in Ontario at the Union. It did not include the right or
privilege of separate schools to teach secondary school courses
with public funding, or to be exempt from school rates for
public secondary school education. This was decided by the Tiny
case.

The final condition indicates that the prohibition in s.
93(1) is against legislation which "prejudicially affects"
rather than just "affects" denominational rights: Ottawa
Separate School Trustees v. City of Ottawa (1916),
1916 CanLII 419 (UK JCPC)
, 32 D.L.R.
10, [1917] A.C. 76. This is sometimes a difficult distinction
to make: see Re Essex County Roman Catholic Separate School
Board and Porter et al. (1978),
1978 CanLII 1323 (ON CA)
, 21 O.R. (2d) 255, 89 D.L.R.
(3d) 445, and Re Essex County Roman Catholic Separate School
Board and Tremblay-Webster et al. (1984),
1984 CanLII 2138 (ON CA)
, 45 O.R. (2d) 83, 5
D.L.R. (4th) 665, 84 C.L.L.C. para. 14030, respecting the
dismissal of separate school teachers who married outside the
Roman Catholic Church.

In the Minority Language Reference, this Court concluded that
the implementation of minority language education rights under

s. 23
of the
Charter
would not unconstitutionally interfere
with the rights of Roman Catholics under s. 93(1).

Section 93(2) guarantees to the dissentient schools of the
Protestants and Roman Catholics in Quebec the same powers,
privileges and duties conferred and imposed at the Union by law
in Upper Canada on the Roman Catholic separate schools and
school trustees. In our opinion s. 93(2) is not pertinent to
the issue before this Court. The fact that the Protestant
minority in Quebec may have had broader privileges at the time
of Confederation cannot be the basis for contending that s.
93(1) embraced the full funding of separate schools in Ontario.
In our opinion s. 93(2) imposed a specific obligation only in
the Province of Quebec. Section 93(1) applies to all of the
provinces which were part of the Union in 1867 and must be
interpreted independently of s. 93(2): see Quebec Ass'n of
Protestant School Boards et al. v. A.-G. Que. et al. (1985),
1985 CanLII 3147 (QC CS)
, 21
D.L.R. (4th) 36 at p. 63, [1985] Que. S.C. 872.

Section 93(3) does not expand the rights and privileges
protected by s. 93(1). What it does is to provide a right of
appeal to the Governor-General in Council from provincial acts
or decisions, whether administrative or legislative, which
affect such rights or privileges. The fact that
s. 93(3)
refers
not only to an existing system of separate or dissentient
schools but also to one "thereafter established" does not alter
the situation. The words "thereafter established" would apply
to a province such as Manitoba or Newfoundland which
established a system of separate schools after Confederation:
see Brophy et al. v. A.-G. Man., to which we have already
referred.

Section 93(3) is broader than s. 93(1). To get relief under

s. 93(3)
, the act or decision only has to affect, not
prejudicially affect, the right or privilege. Furthermore, it
only has to be a right or privilege in relation to education,
not a right or privilege with respect to denominational schools
which a class of persons has by law. It does not have to raise
a matter of legality which could be challenged in the courts on
the ground of ultra vires. It may relate to administrative
impropriety. The rights and privileges under s. 93(1) are given
by law and redress can only be sought from the courts: Tiny
case, Privy Council decision, at pp. 756-9 D.L.R., pp. 369-73
A.C.

Section 93(4) provides machinery for making the decision of
the Governor-General in Council under
s. 93(3)
effective.

So far as legal rights are concerned, in our opinion s. 93(1)
is not an expandable guarantee. After Confederation and until
the
Charter
came into force, the province could by legislation
or regulation expand the rights and privileges of Roman
Catholics with respect to separate schools, but it could not
expand the guarantee which was given by s. 93(1). The only
rights and privileges which were entrenched and which must not
be prejudicially affected were those which existed by law in
the province at the Union with respect to denominational
schools. Subject to this limitation, it could adapt its
educational system to meet the changing needs of society:
Minority Language Reference, at p. 49 O.R., pp. 538-9 D.L.R.
Accordingly there was no legal bar to providing funding for
grades 9 and 10 of Roman Catholic separate schools and it is
not in issue on this reference.

In considering the question whether the guarantee under s.
93(1) is an expandable guarantee, it is of assistance to
compare the provisions of the Constitution and of the
Charter

respecting language rights.

Express provision was made for the use of the English and
French languages in
s. 133
of the
Constitution Act, 1867
. In
dealing with the official languages of Canada in
s. 16(1)
and

(2)
of the
Charter
,
s. 16(3)
expressly provides:

16(3) Nothing in this charter limits the authority of
Parliament or a legislature to advance the equality of status
or use of English and French.

If it had been intended that s. 93(1) should be an expandable
guarantee, a provision similar to s. 16(3) could have been
included in the
Charter
with respect to denominational schools.

IV.  BINDING EFFECT OF THE TINY DECISION

The proponents of Bill 30 contend that the Tiny case was
wrongly decided and ask this Court, notwithstanding that
decision, to hold that the full funding of Roman Catholic
separate schools was included in the guarantee of s. 93(1).

It is to be remembered that when the decision of the Judicial
Committee of the Privy Council in the Tiny case was given, it
was the court of last resort for appeals from Ontario. Under
the doctrine of stare decisis, its decision was binding on this
Court. In a learned article "Stare Decisis at Common Law and
under the Civil Code of Quebec", 31 Can. Bar Rev. 723 (1953),
Professor Wolfgang Friedmann stated at pp. 730-1:

... the abolition of the appeal jurisdiction of the Privy
Council removes the formal authority of the Privy Council in
constitutional matters from the date of the abolition of its
appeal jurisdiction. On the other hand, it does not affect
the authority of its earlier decisions until and unless the
Supreme Court of Canada, in its new role of sovereign and
ultimate court of appeal for Canada, chooses to depart from
them.

A prior decision, particularly in the area of constitutional
law, will be overruled only in rare circumstances. The Privy
Council itself has said that while it was not bound by its own
decisions, nevertheless "on constitutional questions it must be
seldom indeed that the Board would depart from a previous
decision which it may be assumed will have been acted on both
by governments and subjects": A.-G. Ont. et al. v. Canada
Temperance Federation et al.,
1946 CanLII 351 (UK JCPC)
, [1946] 2 D.L.R. 1 at p. 6, [1946]
A.C. 193 at p. 206, 85 C.C.C. 225. The Supreme Court of Canada
has acknowledged that the traditional justification for the
stare decisis principle is certainty in the law and that this
remains an important consideration. It has also indicated that
compelling reasons must exist before it will overturn one of
its prior decisions: Capital Cities Communications Inc. et al.
v. Canadian Radio-television Com'n et al.,
1977 CanLII 12 (SCC)
, [1978] 2 S.C.R. 141
at p. 161, 81 D.L.R. (3d) 609 at p. 622, 36 C.P.R. (2d) 1;
Minister of Indian Affairs & Northern Development v. Ranville
et al.,
1982 CanLII 202 (SCC)
, [1982] 2 S.C.R. 518 at p. 527, 139 D.L.R. (3d) 1 at p.
8, 44 N.R. 616.

The validity of the Privy Council decision in the Tiny case
was not impugned in the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada
in A.-G. Que. v. Greater Hull School Board et al.,
1984 CanLII 29 (SCC)
, [1984] 2
S.C.R. 575, 15 D.L.R. (4th) 651, 28 M.P.L.R. 146. In that case,
actions had been brought to have certain sections of an Act of
the Quebec Legislature respecting municipal taxation declared
unconstitutional. The legislation created a new system of
school financing based on government grants. The Supreme Court
of Canada held that the provisions were ultra vires as they
prejudicially affected rights relating to denominational
schools guaranteed by
s. 93
. As regards financing, the law gave
school commissioners and trustees the right to receive grants
on a proportionate basis and the right to levy taxes from their
respective electors within the limits of "their respective
municipalities". The provisions were held to be ultra vires
because they omitted to state that the grants must be
distributed on a proportionate basis, and because in a
referendum the will of a school board could be subject to the
will of electors not within their districts. Chouinard J., who
delivered the judgment of the majority, cited at p. 584 S.C.R.,
p. 658 D.L.R., and again at p. 594 S.C.R., p. 666 D.L.R., the
Privy Council decision in the Tiny case without in any way
suggesting expressly or impliedly that it was wrong.

It would not be appropriate for this Court at this date to
review the decision of the Judicial Committee in the Tiny case.
We regard the Privy Council decision as binding upon us: Quebec
Ass'n of Protestant School Boards et al. v. A.-G. Que. et al.,
supra, at p. 76. We also note that the majority of this Court
in their judgment have concluded that it is not necessary to
express an opinion on the continuing validity of the Tiny case
and have assumed that it is binding on them.

We dealt earlier under headings II and III with the highly
detailed argument presented by the proponents of Bill 30 in
support of the contention, which was basic to their position on
most aspects of this reference, that the Tiny case was wrongly
decided and ought not to be followed. Subsequent to the
hearing, we were furnished with a list of documents which were
before this Court but which may not have been before Rose J. in
the Tiny case, and a list of documents which it is not certain
were before Rose J. in their entirety. We were also furnished
with a copy of the case on appeal to the Supreme Court of
Canada in the Tiny case.

We are not persuaded that the limited additional material
which is before us and perhaps was not before Rose J. would
have led the courts in the Tiny case to any different
conclusion as to the status of separate schools at the time of
Confederation or as to their entitlement to funding beyond the
elementary level. All of this material, and no doubt more, was
available to the parties to the Tiny  case and to the
distinguished counsel who represented them. So far as factual
determinations are concerned, it must be borne in mind that
they were made some 60 years nearer to Confederation than
today. Our distance of well over a century cannot help but work
as a prism refracting all one wishes to perceive.
