If it were now open to this Court to reverse the Tiny case or
refuse to follow it, we would think it none the less
inappropriate to do so. Until this reference, that case has
been acted upon as standing for the proposition that the
funding of Roman Catholic secondary schools is a matter, not of
constitutional right, but of government policy. The single
purpose sought to be achieved here by changing the law and
thereby transforming the government policy of Bill 30 into a
constitutional right is to avoid requiring Bill 30 to be tested
against the provisions of the
Charter
. To now change the law as
it existed when the Charter came into force solely to except
governmental action from constitutionally entrenched values, we
think would be wrong. In our opinion, this could only serve to
depreciate the Charter rights of citizens of this province and
diminish the worth of the Charter.

V  IS BILL 30 SHIELDED FROM SCRUTINY UNDER THE CHARTER BY S.
29?

The proponents of Bill 30 argue that any right or privilege
given to Roman Catholic separate schools by post-Confederation
legislation enacted either before or after the
Charter
by the
province under its s. 93 power to make laws in relation to
education is shielded from scrutiny under the Charter by the
application of s. 29. This section of the Charter provides
that:

29. Nothing in this
Charter
abrogates or derogates from any
rights or privileges guaranteed by or under the Constitution
of Canada in respect of denominational, separate or
dissentient schools.

We have already expressed the view that neither s. 93(1) nor

s. 93(3)
of the
Constitution Act, 1867
can be seen as
expandable guarantees. Section 93(1) protects only rights and
privileges had "by Law ... at the Union".
Section 93(3)
does
not expand upon those rights or privileges. This section simply
provides a political avenue of redress applicable to separate
or dissentient school systems existing at the Union or
thereafter established with respect to provincial acts or
decisions affecting any right or privilege of a Protestant or
Roman Catholic minority in relation to education. It neither
creates nor guarantees rights or privileges of Roman Catholics
with respect to separate schools.

Section 29 is specifically made applicable only to the
constitutionally guaranteed rights (and we include therein
privileges) of separate schools. It serves to preserve those
rights by ensuring that they are immune from
Charter
attack
notwithstanding that they may contravene the Charter. Section
29 does not create new rights or expand existing rights; in
Ontario, it preserves and protects
s. 93
rights. And the rights
guaranteed by that section are expressly limited to those "with
respect to Denominational Schools which any Class of Persons
have by Law in the Province at the Union": Minority Language
Reference, at p. 44 O.R., pp. 533-4 D.L.R.; R. v. Big M Drug
Mart Ltd.,
1985 CanLII 69 (SCC)
, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 295 at p. 303, 18 D.L.R. (4th) 321
at p. 328, 18 C.C.C. (3d) 385.

The parties supporting Bill 30 do not dispute that the word
"by" in the phrase "any rights or privileges guaranteed by
or under the Constitution of Canada" refers to
s. 93
. It is the
only section in the packet of documents which constitutes the
"Constitution of Canada" (
s. 52(2)
[of the Constitution Act,
1982]), that guarantees any rights or privileges of separate
schools in Ontario. The only rights guaranteed by
s. 93
are, as
we have said, those specified in s. 93(1) -- the denominational
rights which existed in law at Confederation. Section 29
confirms that those s. 93(1) rights have clear primacy over the

Charter
. But public funding of separate secondary schools is
not, as Tiny has established, a right guaranteed by s. 93(1).
It would therefore follow that s. 29 cannot operate to protect
Bill 30 from Charter scrutiny.

To avoid this result and preclude the Court from inquiring
into whether Bill 30 meets the standards of the
Charter
, the
Attorney-General and those in support of his position fasten on
the words "or under" as they appear in s. 29. Their submission
was succinctly put in these terms:

... as a result of the inclusion in section 29 of the Charter
of the words "by or under the Constitution", section 29
protects not only denominational rights guaranteed by
section
93
of the
Constitution Act, 1867
but also those rights given
to denominational schools by post-Confederation legislation
validly enacted by the provinces, including Bill 30.

As the argument goes, if it were intended to provide protection
from the
Charter
only to denominational rights guaranteed by s.
93(1), the words "or under" would be unnecessary since those
rights would already have been protected by the words "by
... the Constitution". Therefore, the section is not confined
to rights that had crystallized at Confederation, and the words
"or under" must protect denominational rights acquired
thereafter. The submission, plainly put, is that any rights or
privileges given to separate schools at any time after 1867,
including after the Charter, by legislation enacted by the
province under the authority granted to it by s. 93 to make
laws in relation to education, are immune from Charter
scrutiny.

The proponents of Bill 30 draw support for this
interpretation of s. 29 from certain statements made during the
course of the proceedings before the Special Joint Committee of
the Senate and of the House of Commons on the Constitution of
Canada. It is important to appreciate the background against
which those statements were made. The Charter as originally
proposed did not include s. 29 or any comparable section. As a
result, the Denominational Education Committees of Newfoundland
became concerned that the guarantees of Term 17 of the Terms of
Union of Newfoundland with Canada [Newfoundland Act, 1949
(U.K.), c. 22], safeguarding denominational rights in that
province might be jeopardized by the then proposed
Charter
.
These concerns were set forth in a brief to the Special Joint
Committee which, by way of summary, concluded:

It must be remembered that the agreement which brought
Newfoundland into the Canadian federation was a solemn
covenant between two proud peoples. Paramount amongst the
concerns of Newfoundlanders at that time was the safeguarding
of their denominational public school system. Without such
assurance, it is most unlikely that the Union would have been
effected. To deny or jeopardize that guarantee, whether
directly or by judicial interpretation in generations to
come, is tantamount to a betrayal of trust.

Both the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice have,
in public statements, assured the people of Newfoundland that
it is not intended that the Constitution Act 1980 will
adversely affect existing denominational rights in education,
now constitutionally entrenched. The Denominational Education
Committees of Newfoundland accept that statement of intention
but respectfully submit that, in order to implement that
intention in future practice so as to preserve intact the
present group rights of denominational education, more
explicit wording must be included in the proposed
Charter of
Rights
.

(Emphasis added: see Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence of the
Special Joint Committee of the Senate and of the House of
Commons on the Constitution of Canada, Issue No. 35, Appendix
"CCC-12".) It is to be noted that these representations
speak to "existing" or "present" denominational rights and not
to future denominational rights. To ensure that the perceived
problem would not occur, the Denominational Education
Committees in their brief suggested a draft amendment to the

Charter
which also speaks to existing rights. It reads:

Any right or privilege with respect to denominational,
separate or dissentient schools granted or secured under

section 93
of the
Constitution Act, 1867
, (formerly named the
British North American Act, 1867), as amended, or under any
provision of the Constitution of Canada in substitution
thereof, shall be a right or freedom guaranteed by the

Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
. The guarantee in
this Charter of certain rights and freedoms shall not be
construed or interpreted as abrogating or derogating from any
right or privilege with respect to denominational, separate
or dissentient schools granted or secured under section 93 of
the Constitution Act, 1867, (formerly named the British North
America Act, 1867), as amended, or under any provision of the
Constitution of Canada in substitution thereof.

(Emphasis added.) As a result of these representations, an
amendment was proposed by a member of the Special Committee to
add as s. 27 (later s. 29) of the
Charter
the following:

27. No provision of this
Charter
affects or abrogates or
derogates from Section 17 of the Schedule to the Newfoundland
Act.

This amendment was further amended to contain the wording of
the present s. 29.

During the discussion on the latter amendment several
statements were made which the proponents contend show that s.
29 was intended to cover legislation such as Bill 30. The gist
of the statements upon which they rely can be seen from the
following excerpt:

Mr. Chairman, the government believes the rights of religious
schools in the various provinces, including Newfoundland,
will not be adversely affected by the
Charter
provisions.

However we want to leave no room for doubt on this issue ...

Mr. Chairman, I point out in the amendment we move the words
"abrogates or derogates from any rights or privileges
guaranteed by or under the Constitution of Canada" -- "under"
meaning the authority of the constitution of Canada; and
therefore any provincial statute or legislation which gives
religious schools rights in the provinces would be protected
from any challenge by the
Charter
by the very nature of the
fact that provincial legislation ultimately flows from the
authority granted to the provinces in the constitution.

(Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence, Issue No. 48, pp. 127-8.)

The status of Ontario legislation affecting separate schools
enacted prior to the
Charter
is not the concern of this
reference and was not the subject of argument. Our concern is
with legislation to be enacted after the Charter came into full
force and effect, and it is to such legislation that we direct
our attention.

With deference to those who think otherwise, we cannot accept
that the word "under" imports the broad and all-encompassing
consequences attributed to it. We reject the notion that every
future piece of legislation enacted by the province under
s. 93

which confers rights or privileges on Roman Catholic separate
schools is placed by s. 29 beyond the purview of the
Charter
.
In our opinion, this Charter provision cannot properly be
construed so as to sweep within its ambit all those statutory
enactments with respect to separate schools which may at some
future time be passed by the Legislature pursuant to its
plenary power over education simply because the Legislature is
acting within its legislative competence.

To be protected by s. 29, the rights and privileges must be
constitutionally guaranteed. The assertion that the phrase
"rights or privileges guaranteed by or under the
Constitution of Canada" covers "rights or privileges granted by
laws enacted under the authority of the Constitution"
disregards s. 29's command that the rights or privileges
themselves be guaranteed. A guarantee does not attach to rights
or privileges conferred by an ordinary provincial statute;
these rights or privileges in no sense become entrenched. While
the province's exclusive authority to legislate in relation to
education is guaranteed, the content of its legislation is not
guaranteed, constitutionally or otherwise. To accept the
proponent's position is tantamount to saying that if the
province grants Roman Catholic separate schools new rights in
addition to those guaranteed by s. 93(1) (and these rights need
not be restricted to those held by public schools), they become
"guaranteed under the Constitution". Therefore, not only are
they free from
Charter
examination but, being now "guaranteed
under the Constitution", they assume the attributes of s. 93(1)
rights and cannot be prejudicially affected. In the case of
Bill 30, this means that the rights granted by it to Roman
Catholic secondary schools, even though not guaranteed by s.
93(1), will become guaranteed because they were granted
pursuant to the province's general authority over education
and, therefore, cannot be prejudicially affected by subsequent
provincial educational enactments. The language of the section
cannot justify that conclusion or the interpretation from which
it follows.

In our opinion, s. 29 does not authorize the creation of new
rights nor does it elevate provincial statutes creating such
rights to constitutional status. If that had been the intent of
the
Charter
, a clear and explicit form of words could readily
have been devised to make that result manifest. As it is, the
section ensures that those rights guaranteed by s. 93(1) and
those rights guaranteed under the various Acts subsequent to
1867, which now by
s. 52(2)
have come to form part of the
"Constitution of Canada", are not abrogated or derogated
from by the Charter. The words used, given their plain and
ordinary meaning, cannot be read so as to embrace rights
created by post-Charter provincial enactments. Furthermore, to
accept that s. 29 renders a statute immune from the Charter
solely because it was enacted within the authority of the
Legislature is to interpret the section in a manner directly
contrary to
s. 32(1)(b)
of the Charter which makes it
abundantly clear that the Charter applies to "all matters
within the authority of the legislature of each province".

The words "en vertu de" in the French version of s. 29 do not
support the position that s. 29 was intended to shield
legislation such as Bill 30 from scrutiny under the
Charter
.
The word "garantis" precedes the words "en vertu de" and cannot
be ignored. It is only rights or privileges which are
constitutionally guaranteed that are protected by s. 29. The
words "or under" are not sufficient by themselves to give
rights or privileges created by legislation enacted under s.
93(1) since the Charter the status of being constitutionally
guaranteed. With deference to the majority, in our opinion,
neither the French or English wording of s. 29 supports their
interpretation or justifies stretching the section to the
extreme that it exempts, as they say, "not only constitutional
guarantees of rights or privileges in respect of
denominational, separate or dissentient schools, but also those
provided by a law enacted pursuant to constitutional authority"
[post, p. 572].

As to the historical development of s. 29, it appears evident
that it was never intended that existing guaranteed
denominational rights would become subject to the
Charter
. The
framers of the earlier draft Charter apparently did not
consider it necessary to make provision for this result. As a
matter of law, the Charter could not, even without s. 29,
abrogate or derogate from the rights guaranteed by other
provisions of the Constitution of Canada. Section 29 was added
out of an abundance of caution to allay the concerns expressed
by the Newfoundland Denominational Education Committees with
respect to constitutionally entrenched denominational rights in
Newfoundland as they existed at that time. We do not read the
proceedings of the Special Joint Committee as manifesting an
intention to free post-Charter provincial legislation from
compliance with the Charter. If that were the intent, the words
used in the section do not achieve their objective.
Furthermore, it is to be borne in mind that in interpreting the
Charter the Court is not to be governed by speeches before the
Special Joint Committee. The minutes of its proceedings are
entitled to no more than minimal weight. As the Supreme Court
of Canada in Reference re s. 94(2) of the Motor Vehicle Act
(R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 288, as amended) (unreported, December
17, 1985 [now reported
1985 CanLII 81 (SCC)
, 23 C.C.C. (3d) 289 at p. 306]), speaking
through Lamer J., recently had occasion to say:

... the Minutes of the Proceedings of the Special Joint
Committee, though admissible, and granted somewhat more
weight than speeches, should not be given too much weight.
The inherent unreliability of such statements and speeches is
not altered by the mere fact that they pertain to the
Charter
of Rights
rather than a statute.

. . . . .

Were this Court to accord any significant weight to this
testimony, it would in effect be assuming a fact which is
nearly impossible of proof, i.e., the intention of the
legislative bodies which adopted the
Charter
. In view of the
indeterminate nature of the data, it would in my view be
erroneous to give these materials anything but minimal
weight.

See also A.-G. Victoria et al. v. Commonwealth of Australia et
al. (1981), 33 A.L.R. 321 (High Court of Australia), per
Barwick C.J. at p. 325.

Finally on this point, we are constrained to observe that any
exception to the
Charter
should be treated cautiously and with
circumspection. If any doubt exists as to whether an exception
to the guaranteed fundamental rights and freedoms is authorized
by the Charter, the doubt must be resolved in favour of the
application of the Charter and not the extension of the
exception. Much was said during the hearing about the Charter
being a "living tree" whose growth ought not to be stunted by
narrow technical interpretations. In our opinion, the
consequences that flow from the construction the proponents of
Bill 30 would have the Court place on the words "or under" run
contrary to the spirit of that concept. To accept that in this
post-Charter era of our constitutional development Bill 30 can
escape scrutiny under the Charter on that narrow technical
basis, in our view, is to give the clock's hands a backward
turn.

VI  IS BILL 30 INCONSISTENT WITH S. 2(a) OR S. 15(1) OF THE
CHARTER?

This brings us to the provisions of
ss. 2(a)
and
15(1)
of the

Charter
upon which the opponents of Bill 30 base their
challenge to the constitutional validity of the proposed
legislation. These sections read as follows:

2. Everyone has the following fundamental freedoms:

(a)  freedom of conscience and religion;

. . . . .

15(1) Every individual is equal before and under the law
and has the right to the equal protection and equal benefit
of the law without discrimination and, in particular, without
discrimination based on race, national or ethnic origin,
colour, religion, sex, age or mental or physical disability.

Prior to the enactment of the
Charter
, Bill 30 would
undoubtedly have constituted a valid exercise of provincial
legislative authority under
s. 93
. The province's plenary power
over education was then limited only to the extent that it
could not pass laws prejudicially affecting those rights or
privileges which existed by law with respect to denominational
schools in the province at the time of Confederation. After
Confederation and before the Charter, there was no
constitutional impediment to the creation of new rights or
privileges for the benefit of separate schools or to the
expansion or enlargement of existing rights or privileges.
This, however, is no longer the case; the rules of the game
have changed. The Charter imposes new limitations on the
province's power over education. Now, legislation applicable to
both public school and separate school education must, unless
otherwise constitutionally mandated, be measured against the
rights and freedoms guaranteed by the Charter. The Charter has
established a new relationship between the individual and the
State. Its text marks the metes and bounds of governmental
authority and individual autonomy. It has been made part of the
Constitution of Canada and, as such, forms part of the supreme
law of Canada. By virtue of
s. 52(1)
of the Constitution Act,
1982, any law inconsistent with the Charter's provisions is, to
the extent of the inconsistency, of no force or effect.

The merits and benefits of Roman Catholic separate schools in
Ontario are not in issue in this reference, nor is the role
that the separate school system has played in the life of this
province. The sole question before this Court is whether State
funding of Roman Catholic separate schools as proposed by Bill
30 can be squared with the dictates of the
Charter
. To answer
this question we turn first to
s. 15(1)
of the Charter which,
pursuant to s. 32(2), came into force on April 17, 1985.

Section 15(1) is a unique guarantee of equality. It covers
not only "equality before the law" and "equal protection of the
law" (clauses which have received interpretation in Canadian,
English and American jurisprudence), but it goes further and
guarantees the right of every individual to both "equality
under the law" and "equal benefit of the law". This variety of
formulations of the concept of equality reflects the intent of
the framers of the
Charter
that s. 15(1) govern the application
of every law so as to ensure that every individual receives the
equal protection and the equal benefit of the law without
discrimination. It appears clear that the language of s. 15(1)
was calculated to avoid the interpretive difficulties that had
been presented by the "equality before the law" clause in s.
1(b) of the Canadian Bill of Rights and to overcome the
restrictions that had attached to that clause: see generally,
Gold, "A Principled Approach to Equality Rights: A Preliminary
Inquiry", 4 Supreme Court L.R. 131 (1982); Hogg, Constitutional
Law of Canada, 2nd ed. (1985), c. 35; and Tarnopolsky, "The
Equality Rights in the Canadian Charter of Rights and
Freedoms", 61 Can. Bar Rev. 242 (1983).

We think it manifest that s. 15(1) must be given a large and
liberal interpretation, one aimed at fulfilling the purpose of
its broad equality guarantee and constraining governmental
action inconsistent with its intent. It must also be
interpreted, and particularly so in dealing with religion, so
as to give full effect to
s. 27
of the
Charter
which recognizes
the multicultural mosaic of contemporary Canadian society and
requires that:

27. This Charter shall be interpreted in a manner
consistent with the preservation and enhancement of the
multicultural heritage of Canadians.

The general approach to be adopted is that enunciated in R. v.
Big M Drug Mart Ltd., supra, at p. 344 S.C.R., pp. 359-60
D.L.R., where Chief Justice Dickson said:

In Hunter v. Southam Inc.,
1984 CanLII 33 (SCC)
, [1984] 2 S.C.R. 145, this Court
expressed the view that the proper approach to the definition
of the rights and freedoms guaranteed by the
Charter
was a
purposive one. The meaning of a right or freedom guaranteed
by the Charter was to be ascertained by an analysis of the
purpose of such a guarantee; it was to be understood, in
other words, in the light of the interests it was meant to
protect.

In my view this analysis is to be undertaken, and the
purpose of the right or freedom in question is to be sought
by reference to the character and the larger objects of the

Charter
itself, to the language chosen to articulate the
specific right or freedom, to the historical origins of the
concepts enshrined, and where applicable, to the meaning and
purpose of the other specific rights and freedoms with which
it is associated within the text of the Charter. The
interpretation should be, as the judgment in Southam
emphasizes, a generous rather than a legalistic one, aimed at
fulfilling the purpose of the guarantee and securing for
individuals the full benefit of the Charter's protection.

In our view, s. 15(1) read as a whole constitutes a
compendious expression of a positive right to equality in both
the substance and the administration of the law. It is an all-
encompassing right governing all legislative action. Like
the ideals of "equal justice" and "equal access to the law",
the right to equal protection and equal benefit of the law now
enshrined in the
Charter
rests on the moral and ethical
principle fundamental to a truly free and democratic society
that all persons should be treated by the law on a footing of
equality with equal concern and equal respect.

This is not to suggest that s. 15(1) requires that every
person in every instance be treated in precisely the same
manner. There is no infringement of the section unless the
unequal treatment is discriminatory. Most laws provide for
distinctions and prescribe different results based on those
distinctions. Indeed, a State could not function without
classifying its citizens for various purposes and treating some
differently from others. As Mr. Justice Stewart pointed out in
his discussion of the equal protection clause of the U.S.
Fourteenth Amendment in San Antonio School District v.
Rodriguez (1973), 411 U.S. 1 at p. 60: "There is hardly a law
on the books that does not affect some people differently from
others." Similarly, although spoken in a different context,
Chief Justice Dickson said at p. 347 S.C.R., p. 362 D.L.R. of
Big M Drug Mart Ltd., supra, "... the interests of true
equality may well require differentiation in treatment". This
Court in Re McDonald and The Queen (1985),
1985 CanLII 162 (ON CA)
, 51 O.R. (2d) 745 at
p. 765, 21 D.L.R. (4th) 397 at p. 417, 21 C.C.C. (3d) 330,
speaking through Morden J.A., accepted that "[i]t can
reasonably be said, in broad terms, that the purpose of s. 15
is to require 'that those who are similarly situated be treated
similarly'." This analysis is appropriate to the subject-matter
of this reference and, so far as the issue arises, can aptly be
applied. However, on the view we take of the relationship
between s. 15(1) and Bill 30, there is no need to consider
either the various tests that have been developed to assess the
legitimacy of particular statutory classifications or the
various approaches that have been suggested with respect to the
application of s. 15(1): see, Gold, "A Principled Approach to
Equality Rights: A Preliminary Inquiry", supra, at pp. 151-3;
Hogg, Constitutional Law of Canada, supra, at pp. 800-1; Re
McDonald and The Queen, at pp. 763-5 O.R., pp. 415-7 D.L.R.

Section 15(1) forbids governments, in respect of all matters
within their legislative authority, from denying to
individuals, and similarly to groups of individuals, the equal
protection and equal benefit of the law on a discriminatory
basis. For greater particularity, the section enumerates
specific prohibited grounds of discrimination. Not
unexpectedly, religion is one. Although religion throughout the
ages has provided spiritual comfort, guidance and inspiration
to its adherents, it holds the potential for divisiveness and,
as history has demonstrated, can serve to divide societies by
discriminating against those whose beliefs are not in accord
with the religions that from time to time may achieve
dominance. If the
Charter
's right to equality without
discrimination on religious grounds is to mean anything, it
must mean at least that the followers of one religion are not
to be the subjects of greater burdens or the beneficiaries of
greater benefits imposed or provided by law than the followers
of other religions. Unless the State can demonstrably justify
its action under
s. 1
of the Charter, it must not be partial in
its dealings with its citizens by favouring one group on the
basis of religion with financial support or other benefits that
are not comparably available to those of other religious
persuasions. In our opinion, Bill 30, by providing benefits on
the basis of religion to one religious group only, is in direct
conflict with the equality guarantee of s. 15(1).

Patently, those rights and privileges that were guaranteed to
Roman Catholic separate schools by
s. 93(1)
of the
Constitution
Act, 1867
, have been preserved by s. 29 and are not subject to

Charter
challenge. If Bill 30 were addressed to such rights or
privileges, its constitutional validity would be unassailable
regardless of whether it violated s. 15(1) or not. But Bill 30
is addressed to matters that are not constitutionally
entrenched. It has been a recognized and accepted fact of
constitutional life in Ontario since the Tiny case that
separate school rights under
s. 93
do not include any
entitlement to public funding beyond the elementary school
level. In 1971, Premier Davis, in the statement adverted to
earlier, spoke of values which now underlie the equal benefit
guarantee when he said that "[to] embark upon such a policy
[full funding of separate schools] could not be, in reason
or justice, limited to some faiths and denied to others". This
conclusion is now compelled by the Charter. Bill 30's proposal
to fully fund the schools of one religion, in the absence of
any constitutional requirement that this be done, without
provision for any funding of other religiously based schools,
is, by any standard of scrutiny, discriminatory and violative
of s. 15(1).

We outlined earlier the provisions of Bill 30 and the scheme
of the proposed legislation under the heading "Bill 30". While,
in our opinion, the over-all purpose of the Bill operates to
render it in its entirety in contravention of s. 15(1), we
shall none the less make brief reference to certain of its
provisions which in themselves contravene s. 15(1).

To implement its aim of providing full funding of secondary
education in Roman Catholic separate schools through to the
completion of grade 13, certain sections of Bill 30 which we
have already discussed, that is, ss. 136e, 136f and 136g, deal
specifically with the entitlement of Roman Catholic school
boards, or in the case of s. 136f, a separate school board, to
a share in the legislative grants for secondary school
purposes. Section 136j exempts separate school supporters
within the area of jurisdiction of a Roman Catholic school
board from payment of all rates imposed for secondary school
purposes of a public board and s. 136k, a companion provision
to s. 136j, makes those separate school supporters liable for
taxes levied for the support of Roman Catholic separate
schools. These provisions, for reasons already stated, clearly
contravene s. 15(1).

The opponents of Bill 30 submit that s. 136x is similarly
invalid. It will be recalled that this section empowers a
tribunal which is appointed by the Planning and Implementation
Commission to transfer from a public board to a Roman Catholic
school board the use or ownership of real or personal property,
or both. There is no provision requiring compensation and the
Expropriations Act, R.S.O., 1980, c. 148, is declared
inapplicable to any such transfer. Provision is made in s.
136x(10) for a retransfer by the Minister with the approval of
the Lieutenant-Governor in Council and certain criteria are
stated as applicable to the tribunal's determination (ss. 136v
and 136x(6)). While it is difficult to see how the compulsory
taking of property of a public school board for the purpose of
a Roman Catholic school board without compensation would not
infringe s. 15(1), in view of the complexity of the scheme and
the criteria attached to it, we think it preferable not to
attempt to interpret s. 136x in the absence of a specific
factual situation. Similarly, with respect to the submissions
as to the discriminatory impact of Bill 30 on teachers and
pupils (ss. 136l and 136o), we are of the view that the record
before this Court is insufficient to permit a conclusion to be
drawn on these significant issues.

In summary, ss. 136e, 136f, 136g, 136j and 136k are at the
heart of Bill 30's proposed full funding of Roman Catholic
secondary schools, and are not severable from the balance of
the Bill. The statute contemplated by this Bill would, if
enacted, provide Roman Catholics with financial benefits on the
basis of their religion that are not available to any extent to
members of other religions. Roman Catholics would become
entitled to receive legislative grants for separate secondary
school purposes; they would be exempt from the payment of rates
imposed for public secondary school purposes; and they would be
able to utilize their tax payments for the support of their
denominational schools. The Bill makes no provision whereby
those of other religious persuasions would become entitled to
any form of public support for schools in which their
respective religions play a similarly important role, and no
government policy in this respect has yet been formulated.
Instead, all non-Roman Catholic parents who wish to educate
their children outside the public school system and in schools
of their respective denominations, would remain obliged to pay
both public school taxes and private school tuition. In these
circumstances, without constitutional sanction for such
preferential treatment, the public support intended by Bill 30
for the education of children of one selected religion, on the
basis of their religion, is at odds with the letter and spirit
of s. 15(1) and, in our opinion, constitutes a direct and
obvious infringement of the guarantee of equal benefit of the
law without discrimination based on religion given by the

Charter
to all Canadians.

Having reached this conclusion, we refrain from expressing an
opinion on the question of whether Bill 30 also infringes the
fundamental freedom of religion guaranteed by
s. 2(a)
of the

Charter
.

VII  CAN BILL 30 BE SAVED BY S. 1 OF THE CHARTER?

We turn now to consider whether, notwithstanding its breach
of s. 15(1), Bill 30 can be saved by
s. 1
of the
Charter
.
Section 1 provides:

1. The
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
guarantees
the rights and freedoms set out in it subject only to such
reasonable limits prescribed by law as can be demonstrably
justified in a free and democratic society.

The principles governing the application of s. 1 were
enunciated by Chief Justice Dickson in R. v. Big M Drug Mart
Ltd., supra, at p. 352 S.C.R., p. 366 D.L.R., as follows:

At the outset, it should be noted that not every government
interest or policy objective is entitled to s. 1
consideration. Principles will have to be developed for
recognizing which government objectives are of sufficient
importance to warrant overriding a constitutionally protected
right or freedom. Once a sufficiently significant government
interest is recognized then it must be decided if the means
chosen to achieve this interest are reasonable -- a form of
proportionality test. The court may wish to ask whether the
means adopted to achieve the end sought to do so by impairing
as little as possible the right or freedom in question.

In this reference, as in all cases where s. 1 must be
applied, the onus of establishing that the violation of the

Charter
is a reasonable limit that is demonstrably justified
rests on the party seeking to uphold the constitutional
validity of the infringing legislation. Here, it is the
Attorney-General who must bear the significant burden of
demonstrating that the objective of Bill 30 is of sufficient
importance to warrant overriding the constitutionally protected
right guaranteed by s. 15(1) to equal benefit of the law
without discrimination based on religion.

In an effort to discharge this onus, counsel for the
Attorney-General and those supporting his position make a
number of submissions. To quote from the Attorney-General's
factum, Bill 30's objective "is to give the same rights to
Catholic schools [as to public schools] so that both branches
of the publicly supported public school system are treated
equally"; and the means chosen to achieve the objective
constitute the "only reasonable approach" to resolution of "the
longstanding historical disparities between the two branches of
the public education system". Referring further to the
Attorney-General's factum, the argument then proceeds, in
short, along these lines: both branches of the common school
system were funded equally before Confederation; it is only
reasonable in view of
s. 93
that they should have been funded
equally since Confederation; separate schools are an integral
part of the Ontario public school system; it is now reasonable
to extend the existing funding to complete equality in the
public education system; Bill 30 is "simply the culmination of
a gradual movement back to the pre-Confederation provision of
equality" between the public and separate school systems; the
disparity in financing suffered by separate schools
demonstrates "the reasonable justification" for now providing
full public funding; the funding is needed to serve the large
Roman Catholic segment of the Ontario public ("a good one third
of our families") who "continue to hold the view that the
education of their children should take place in a Roman
Catholic context"; Bill 30 would remove "the artificial
barriers to Roman Catholic schooling" erected since
Confederation and "redress a longstanding grievance" by
restoring separate schools to pre-Confederation status; it is
"only just and reasonable" that separate schools now begin
"to reap the benefits of the Confederation bargain"; modern
society necessitates a full secondary education; and an
increasing number of Roman Catholic school supporters have been
placed in the "invidious position" of having to choose between
a free non-Catholic public secondary education and a Catholic
secondary education which is partially funded.

With respect to schools of other religions, the Attorney-
General contends that it is reasonable not to extend public
funding to them; to do so could cause the government to have
"no real control over the cost of or fragmentation of the
public education system". Furthermore, the argument goes: "no
religious group other than Roman Catholics have any claim to
historically protected constitutional rights in respect to
education"; the question of whether public funding should be
provided to other religious schools, or to private schools
generally, raises complex educational, fiscal and
administrative problems with respect to which no government
policy has yet been formulated; it would be necessary to
determine whether the public system of education "would be
injured by the draining away of students, teachers and
resources" if public funding were extended to these schools. In
contrast to the problems associated with the introduction of
public support for other denominational schools, Bill 30, it is
said, represents a "relatively modest initiative" which "can be
accomplished without injury to the public school system". On
this basis, it is submitted that Bill 30 is reasonable and
demonstrably justified.

The government's position on s. 1, like its position on the
constitutional validity of Bill 30, is premised in large
measure on the proposition that
s. 93
guarantees separate
schools the same rights to financial support as public schools.
However, if the Tiny case is accepted as the conclusive
interpretation of s. 93, and in our opinion it must be so
accepted, it cannot be validly contended that Roman Catholic
secondary schools have been deprived of public funds to which
they were constitutionally entitled, nor can it be said that
the terms of the "Confederation bargain" have not been
fulfilled. The Tiny case has stood for 60 years as an
authoritative pronouncement that under
s. 93
separate school
rights extend only to the elementary level. On this basis,
successive Ontario governments have been legally entitled not
to provide public funding for separate secondary schools though
empowered to do so. This was clearly the state of the law when
the
Constitution Act, 1982
and the Charter came into force.

In determining whether rights beyond those guaranteed by
s.
93
conferred by post-Charter legislation can, even though in
conflict with the
Charter
, be justified under s. 1, it
contributes little to the resolution of the issue to dwell upon
the structure and content of the educational system as it
existed in the Ontario of 1867 or to stress grievances about
the policies of past provincial governments that cannot
properly be put in question in this forum. The issue must be
decided in the context of the constitutional compact of 1982
and in light of contemporary conditions in this province which
bear little, if any, resemblance to those existing at the time
of Confederation. Today's large Roman Catholic segment of the
population of Ontario can itself hardly be compared in terms of
relative numbers, place of national origin or generally with
1867's small Roman Catholic minority. It is essential also to
recognize, and particularly so in considering legislation in
breach of an equality guarantee on the ground of religious
discrimination, that Ontario today is a multicultural and
pluralistic society composed of people of many diverse social,
ethnic, racial and religious backgrounds. Religion is a
dominant feature of their multicultural heritage and, by the
very terms of the Charter, the multicultural heritage of
Canadians is to be preserved and enhanced.

With this in mind, it cannot be said, as the proponents of
Bill 30 suggest, that, because supporters of separate schools
were constitutionally identified in 1867 as having special
rights whereas supporters of other religious schools were not
so favoured, legislation expanding those rights is entitled to
special treatment under the
Charter
. In our opinion, to the
extent that a benefit is being given beyond that
constitutionally guaranteed by s. 93, Roman Catholics stand in
no different position than those of other religious
persuasions. Bill 30 must therefore be subject to the same
scrutiny under s. 1 as would legislation giving benefits to
followers of any other selected religion.

One can sympathize with Roman Catholic parents who are
compelled by law to pay taxes for public schools but feel
constrained by conscience and discipline to support
denominational schools for their own children. But the same is
equally true of members of other religions whose children also
require a full secondary education. No evidence was presented
to this Court establishing that Roman Catholics, more than
others, hold the view that the education of their children
should take place in a religious environment. Nor was there any
evidence that the "need" for full funding in Roman Catholic
separate schools is any greater than in the schools of other
Christian denominations, or in the schools of other faiths
where religion plays an equally important role. In this regard
it should perhaps be noted that the validation of Bill 30 by s.
1 is opposed by the Ontario Alliance of Christian Schools, by
the Coalition for Public Education Ontario Inc. which includes
the Anglican Church, the Baptist Convention of Ontario and
Quebec, the Presbyterian Church, and the United Church of
Canada, and by the Seventh-Day Adventist Church, the Canadian
Unitarian Council and representatives of the Jewish and Hindu
communities.

In any application of s. 1, an important factor to be
considered in assessing the sufficiency of the governmental
interest is the benefit of the legislation to society at large.
Obviously, if legislation does not clearly and in some
significant respect advance the general public interest, it
cannot justify infringing
Charter
rights and freedoms. Here, no
evidence was presented that Bill 30 will operate to benefit the
public as a whole. The focus was on whether it will fragment
the non-denominational education system and impair its
viability. Counsel for the Attorney-General points to the
provisions designed to protect teachers and pupils from
foreseeable adverse consequences and contends that full funding
"can be accomplished without injury to the public school
system". On the other hand, opponents of Bill 30 submit that
full funding represents much more than the fine tuning of an
existing system; huge sums of public money and, presumably,
public property are involved and, they say, the legislation
will have a very serious detrimental effect on the entire
public school system and on the non-sectarian teaching
profession.

No studies or reports have been presented from which any
definitive conclusion can be drawn as to how either Bill 30 or
the funding of other religious schools will impact on the
present system of public education in the province. Nor has
consideration been given in light of the values recognized by
the
Charter
to the desirability of extending State support, or
further State support, to the denominational education of any
religion. While the government appointed a commission on
private schools in Ontario (the Shapiro Commission), the
report, issued subsequent to the hearing, is not a part of
these proceedings. As matters presently stand, no government
policy has yet been formulated which takes into account the
reality that denominational schools other than Roman Catholic
exist in Ontario or which seeks to accommodate the Charter
rights of supporters of those schools or promote the proclaimed
objective of s. 27 to preserve and enhance the multicultural
heritage of Canadians.

Finally, one further submission on behalf of the Attorney-
General should be noted. Bill 30, it is argued, "is not
simply a government Bill but is legislation supported by all
three political parties" and in this "unique situation" the
Court "should be reluctant to substitute its opinion for that
of the Legislative Assembly" and should "in the circumstances"
declare the Bill to be a reasonable limit on
Charter
rights.

We find that submission untenable. The agreement of political
parties stands on no higher plane than the Legislature's
approbation of all provincially enacted statutes that come
before the courts by way of
Charter
review. The very purpose of
the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms is to declare
certain values transcendent and beyond the reach of political
majorities. The majoritarian process cannot be expected to
rectify claims that arise as a response to that very
majoritarian process. The Court, in the discharge of its
responsibility as a guardian of the Charter, must be faithful
to its content and ensure that the rights and freedoms
guaranteed by the Charter are honoured.

On the material before this Court, we are of the opinion that
the Attorney-General has not discharged the burden of
demonstrating that Bill 30's violation of
Charter
rights can be
justified under s. 1. The benefit to be provided by the
proposed legislation solely on the ground of religion to one
religiously based educational system without any provision for
the funding of or support to other religiously based schools is
not a reasonable limit on the equality guarantee.

VIII  CONCLUSION

In the result therefore we would answer the question put to
the Court in the affirmative. Bill 30 provides a discriminatory
unequal benefit and for that reason is inconsistent with
s.
15(1)
of the
Charter
and has not been justified under s. 1. In
our opinion, Bill 30 would in its entirety be of no force or
effect if enacted.

The provincial legislature is supreme in matters of
education, excepting so far as s. 93 of the B.N.A. Act
restricts its authority. Subsection 1 preserves as they stood
any rights and the privileges given in relation to
denominational schools by law in 1867. The question,
therefore, is whether the Province could then as the law
stood so control the courses of study and the general range
and quality of the textbooks used, as to enable the
educational authorities of the Province to prescribe the
gradation of the separate school and the stages in which
instruction should be given in it.

They then went on to hold, at pp. 770-1 D.L.R., pp. 387-8 A.C.,
that the province had the power to regulate courses of study
and gradation of schools and to apportion funds for approved
courses of study and grades. At p. 772 D.L.R., p. 389 A.C.,
they asserted:

Their Lordships do not think grading is in itself
inconsistent with such rights to separation of schools as
were reserved at Confederation.

Now if we were to ignore for a moment the Tiny decision and
examine the applicable legislation in effect in 1867 -- Common
Schools Act, C.S.U.C. 1859, c. 64; Separate Schools Act, 1863
(U.C.), c. 5 (Scott Act), and Grammar Schools Act, 1865
(U.C.), c. 23 -- one could observe that:

(1) it was the "duty" of trustees of common (and therefore of
separate) schools to permit all residents aged 5 to 21 to
attend school (s. 27(16) Common Schools Act; s. 9 of the
Separate Schools Act);

(2) no text could be used which was disapproved by the Council
of Public Instruction and, if disapproved, no portion of the
Legislative School Grant could be applied to that school (s.
128, Common Schools Act),

(3) the separate schools were to receive a share of the
legislative grant proportionate to the average number of pupils
attending such schools (s. 20, Separate Schools Act);

(4) there was nothing in the Grammar Schools Act to the effect
that those schools were given exclusive rights or funding to
provide secondary school education.

If, in addition, one were to consider that textbooks used in
separate and common schools indicate study at the highest pre-
university levelWith respect to courses of study see
Hodgins, in Documentary History of Education in Upper Canada,
vol. 23, c. VII, "Programme of Studies for Public Schools,
1871" pp. 83-7, and c. IX at pp. 114-6. With respect to texts
used see Suppliant's Case, Introducing Exhibits, before the
Supreme Court of Ontario in the Tiny case, supra, pp. 79-82 and
app. H to the Separate School manual of 1863, pp. 304-6, as
well as "The Chief Superintendent's Annual Report of the
Normal, Model, Grammar, Common and Separate Schools in Upper
Canada for the Year 1858" in Historical Educational Papers and
Documents of Ontario, 1842-1861, pp. 257-62. Also see Stamp,
The Schools of Ontario, 1876-1976, p. 7. that graduates of such
schools went directly into university or the learned
professions,See Suppliant's Case, Introducing Exhibits in the
Tiny case before the Supreme Court of Ontario, p. 103. Also see
Stamp, The Schools of Ontario, 1876-1976, p. 7 and Hodgins, The
Establishment of Schools and Colleges in Ontario, v. II, p.
146. and that the Common and Grammar Schools Act, 1871 (Ont.),
c. 33 ["An Act to Improve the Common and Grammar Schools of the
Province of Ontario"], which replaced those schools with
elementary (public) schools and secondary (high) schools, did
not apply to separate schools, one would have to conclude that
secondary school education up to the pre-university level was
being given in separate schools, that the textbooks used were
not disapproved, and that full and equal funding for such
pupils and such grades was being provided by the province.
Other than Duff J. in the Supreme Court of Canada, no judge who
participated in the Tiny decision, came to a contrary
conclusion.

Therefore, even accepting the decision of the Judicial
Committee in Tiny that all these examples of the provision of
secondary school education in the separate schools did not
preclude provincial regulation of the grades to which public
funding would be accorded, it seems clear that by s. 93 the
province can now decide to return to separate schools the
rights they exercised in 1867 to provide secondary school
education and to receive equal proportionate funding for such
education, unless there is something in the
Charter
to preclude
it.

III

The key
Charter
provision that has to be considered is s. 29,
because it relates specifically to the subject at hand. Because
of its critical importance, the English version is repeated
with certain emphasis and the French version, with the same
emphasis, is added.

29. Nothing in this
Charter
abrogates or derogates from any
rights or privileges guaranteed by or under the Constitution
of Canada in respect of denominational, separate or
dissentient schools.

29. Les dispositions de la presente charte ne portent pas
atteinte aux droits ou privileges garantis en vertu de la
Constitution du Canada concernant les ecoles separees et
autres ecoles confessionnelles.

The crucial words in s. 29 are: "any rights or privileges
guaranteed by or under the Constitution of Canada", especially
the words "guaranteed by or under". "Guaranteed by the
Constitution" would appear to refer specifically to s. 93 as
far as concerns the four original provinces, as well as British
Columbia and Prince Edward Island, admitted to the Union
pursuant to
s. 146
. It was urged upon us that the words "or
under" must refer to such other provisions as s. 22 of the
Manitoba Act, 1870 (Can.), c. 33, confirmed by the Constitution
Act, 1871; s. 17 of each of the Alberta Act, 1905 (Can.), c. 3,
and the Saskatchewan Act, 1905 (Can.), c. 42; and Term 17 of
the Terms of Union of Newfoundland with Canada (confirmed by
the Newfoundland Act, 1949 (U.K.), c. 22). However, these four
Acts are listed in the Schedule to the
Constitution Act, 1982

and so, by virtue of
s. 52(2)(b)
, constitute part of the
Constitution of Canada. Therefore, the words, "or under" were
evidently not necessary to cover these situations. Clearly the
words "or under" were intended to cover guarantees other than
those granted by the Constitution. It might be noted that
s. 21

of the Charter which, according to the marginal note, provides
for "continuation of constitutional provisions" with respect to
the English and French languages uses the following terms:

21. Nothing in sections 16 to 20 abrogates or derogates
from any right, privilege or obligation with respect to the
English and French languages, or either of them, that exists
or is continued by virtue of any other provision of the
Constitution of Canada.

(Emphasis added.)

If s. 29 was intended to protect only constitutional rights
and privileges from the
Charter
, the words "by virtue of any
provision of the Constitution of Canada" might have been
expected to be used instead of "by or under the Constitution of
Canada". The words "under the Constitution of Canada" must
include rights and privileges granted by laws enacted under the
authority of the Constitution. This conclusion is supported by
the French version of s. 29 which uses the one term "en vertu
de", which is translated by Le Petit Robert as "par le pourvoir
de", which could be translated as "by the power of ". It is
interesting to note that the French equivalent of the words "by
Law" in
s. 93(1)
of the
Constitution Act, 1867
, is "par la
loi". All of this indicates that the words as used in s. 29
were intended to include not only constitutional guarantees of
rights or privileges in respect of denominational, separate or
dissentient schools, but also those provided by a law enacted
pursuant to constitutional authority.

That this was the intention of the framers of the

Constitution Act, 1982
, is clear from the Proceedings and
Evidence of the Special Joint Committee of the Senate and of
the House of Commons on the Constitution of Canada, 1980-81.

It is interesting to note that s. 29 did not appear in the
initial proposal for the
Charter
in October, 1980. In fact, it
was not added even after the representations made to the
Special Joint Committee during late 1980, pursuant to which the
Minister of Justice proposed a number of amendments on January
14, 1981. The Special Joint Committee had received a brief from
the Joint Executive of the Denominational Education Committees
of Newfoundland on January 9, 1981. The thrust of the brief was
that Term 17 of the Terms of Union of Newfoundland with Canada,
protecting denominational education in Newfoundland, might not
be protected from being overridden by Charter rights. This fear
was expressed as follows, at p. 35A:10 of the proceedings on
January 9, 1981:

It is possible that the Courts, applying Sections 2(a) and
15(1), might interpret them so as to limit or even abrogate
the constitutional rights and privileges guaranteed by Term
17. This is especially so when
Section 1
of the
Charter
is
considered, the section providing that the rights and
freedoms set out in the Charter are "subject only to such
reasonable limits as are generally accepted in a free and
democratic society with a parliamentary system of
government."

This Brief has already made the points that, in applying
these sections, it will be open to the Court to hold that the
British Parliament, in enacting these sections, "intended"
that "reasonable limits" be placed on constitutional
denominational rights in education in the interest of the
civil liberties of individuals and that where the line will
be drawn will be completely dependent on the policy choices
which a majority of the judges of the Supreme Court of Canada
make from time to time on particular issues before them.

Consequently, we repeat that every effort must be taken to
make certain that the rights and privileges of denominational
schools, now included in the Constitution, and intended to be
continued by the Constitution Act, 1980, be explicitly
mentioned and given full weight in the
Charter of Rights
.

Pursuant to the hearing of this brief, on January 29, 1981,
Mr. McGrath, a Newfoundland Conservative member of the Special

Constitution Act which would have added a new section, then
numbered 27 (at p. 48:126):

27. No provision of this
Charter
affects or abrogates or
derogates from Section 17 of the Schedule to the Newfoundland
Act.

Immediately after, however, on behalf of the government,
Senator Petten moved an amendment to the amendment which was
the wording finally adopted and which now constitutes s. 29. At

Mr. Chairman, the government believes the rights of

However, we want to leave no room for doubt on this issue

I might say at the outset that I and my colleagues support

I might add that we would also provide rights to schools,

The Conservative amendment as it stands is too narrow,

But I would like to point out for the benefit of the

Mr. Chairman, I think that pretty well covers my

He understands that it broadens the scope of the amendment

Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

The response to this proposal was made by Mr. McGrath in the
following terms, at pp. 48:128-9:

Mr. McGrath: Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, very briefly, I first of all agree with what
Mr. Tobin has said, that the amendment to the amendment is
acceptable to the Denominational Educational Committees in
Newfoundland. It broadens the scope of it, and indeed it is
well worth recording here that we had representations from
the Roman Catholic School Trustees and representations from
the Roman Catholic Bishops of Ontario; and from the
Protestant School Board of Greater Montreal, and there was
one other -- and they raised concerns about denominational or
separate school rights and the effect the
Charter
would have
on them.

. . . . .

I would like to say in conclusion, Mr. Chairman, that I
would like naturally to thank the government for meeting the

Following a further brief exchange, the members of the
committee adopted unanimously the government version, which is
the present s. 29 (pp. 48:130-1).

What this record clearly indicates is that s. 29 was intended
to protect not only "any rights or privileges guaranteed by ...
the Constitution of Canada", such as those in
s. 93
of the

Constitution Act, 1867
, s. 17 of each of the Alberta Act, 1905
and the Saskatchewan Act, 1905, and Term 17 of the Terms of
Union of Newfoundland with Canada, but also "any rights or
privileges guaranteed ... under the Constitution of Canada",
such as those contained within provincial statutes enacted
pursuant to the plenary power over education in the opening
paragraph of
s. 93
. Bill 30, if enacted, would be one such
statute and so must, at least in its basic purpose and over-all
thrust, receive the protection of s. 29 from any abrogation or
derogation because of any of the rights or freedoms set out in
the
Charter
, including
ss. 2(a)
and
15
.

This construction of
s. 29
of the
Charter
accords not only
with the legislative record, but also with common sense. It
would be a very great irony indeed if the Canadian Charter of
Rights and Freedoms were to operate to abrogate the benefits
that could be extended to a religious minority in the field of
education pursuant to s. 93.

Moreover, as noted earlier, both Ontario and Quebec entered
into Confederation on the condition that the educational rights
of the religious minorities in those provinces were protected.
This was one of the cornerstones of Confederation. The
recognition and protection of the educational rights of the
Protestant minority in Quebec and of the Roman Catholic
minority in Ontario constituted a condition precedent to those
provinces becoming part of Canada. Section 93 of the original

Constitution Act, 1867
gave effect to the bargain, which has
been fulfilled in Quebec. It should not be broken in Ontario.

These educational rights, granted specifically to the
Protestants in Quebec and the Roman Catholics in Ontario, make
it impossible to treat all Canadians equally. The country was
founded upon the recognition of special or unequal educational
rights for specific religious groups in Ontario and Quebec. The
incorporation of the
Charter
into the Constitution Act, 1982,
does not change the original Confederation bargain. A specific
constitutional amendment would be required to accomplish that.

Section 29
of the Charter makes it clear that the minority
education rights (an essential condition of Confederation) are
not to be abrogated by ss. 2(a) or 15.

Without discussing at any length the full ambit of
s. 26
of
the
Charter
, it might be noted that this view of s. 29 accords
with the patent intent of s. 26 as well.

The answer, therefore, to the question referred to this Court
has to be that Bill 30, in its basic purpose and over-all
thrust, is not "inconsistent with the provisions of the
Constitution of Canada including the
Canadian Charter of Rights
and Freedoms
".

This conclusion does not mean, and must not be taken to mean
that separate schools are exempt from the law or the
Constitution. Laws and the Constitution, particularly the

Charter
, are excluded from application to separate schools only
to the extent they derogate from such schools as Catholic (or
in Quebec, Protestant) institutions. It is this essential
Catholic nature which is preserved and protected by
s. 93
of
the
Constitution Act, 1867
and
s. 29
of the Charter. The courts
must strike a balance, on a case-by-case basis, between conduct
essential to the proper functioning of a Catholic school and
conduct which contravenes such Charter rights as those of
equality in s. 15 or of conscience and religion in s. 2(a).
Thus, the right of a Catholic school board to dismiss Catholic
members of its teaching staff for marrying in a civil ceremony,
or for marrying divorced persons, has been upheld as
permissible conduct for a separate school board, but would the
same protection be afforded a board which refused to hire women
or discriminated on the basis of race, national or ethnic
origin, age or disability?

In Re Essex County Roman Catholic Separate School Board and
Porter et al. (1978),
1978 CanLII 1323 (ON CA)
, 21 O.R. (2d) 255, 89 D.L.R. (3d) 445,
this Court upheld the right of a separate school board to
dismiss teachers for "denominational cause" without review by a
board of reference. Zuber J.A. observed at p. 257 O.R., p. 447
D.L.R.:

Serious departures from denominational standards by a teacher
cannot be isolated from his or her teaching duties since
within the denominational school religious instruction,
influence and example form an important part of the
educational process:

In Caldwell et al. v. Stuart et al.,
1984 CanLII 128 (SCC)
, [1984] 2 S.C.R. 603, 15
D.L.R. (4th) 1, [1985] 1 W.W.R. 620, the contract of a Roman
Catholic teacher in British Columbia was not renewed when it
was discovered that she had married a divorced man. The issue
was whether the school was discriminating against Mrs. Caldwell
because of her religion and marital status (prohibited heads of
discrimination under the British Columbia Human Rights Code) or
whether its requirement that Catholic teachers adhere to
Catholic tenets was in fact a bona fide occupational
qualification. The Supreme Court of Canada used a two-tiered
test derived from its earlier decision in Ontario Human Rights
Com'n et al. v. Borough of Etobicoke,
1982 CanLII 15 (SCC)
, [1982] 1 S.C.R. 202 at p.
208, 132 D.L.R. (3d) 14 at pp. 19-20, 82 C.L.L.C. para.
17
,005,
which required that the qualification be imposed (1) honestly,
in good faith and in the sincerely held belief that it is
imposed in the interest of the adequate performance of the
work, and (2) because it was related, in an objective sense, to
the performance of the employment. McIntyre J. stated at pp.
624-5 S.C.R., p. 18 D.L.R.:

The Board found that the Catholic school differed from the
public school. This difference does not consist in the mere
addition of religious training to the academic curriculum.
The religious or doctrinal aspect of the school lies at its
very heart and colours all its activities and programs. The
role of the teacher in this respect is fundamental to the
whole effort of the school, as much in its spiritual nature
as in the academic. It is my opinion that objectively viewed,
having in mind the special nature and objectives of the
school, the requirement of religious conformance including
the acceptance and observance of the Church's rules regarding
marriage is reasonably necessary to assure the achievement of
the objects of the school. It is my view that the Etobicoke
test is thus met and that the requirement of conformance
constitutes a bona fide qualification in respect of the
occupation of a Catholic teacher employed in a Catholic
school, the absence of which will deprive her of the
protection of s. 8 of the Human Rights Code. It will be only
in rare circumstances that such a factor as religious
conformance can pass the test of bona fide qualification. In
the case at bar, the special nature of the school and the
unique role played by the teachers in the attaining of the
school's legitimate objects are essential to the finding that
religious conformance is a bona fide qualification.

In the above cases, the courts were faced with individual
challenges to the authority of separate school boards in
specific circumstances. On a reference such as the present one,
the Court cannot attempt to define the parameters of such
authority nor can it deal effectively with challenges to
particular sections without a clear and precise factual
background. In any event, the individual sections to which
objection was taken are severable and do not pertain to the
critical aspect of the Bill providing for full funding of
separate schools.

The main question before this Court is whether the province
would contravene the Constitution, including the
Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms
, by enacting Bill 30. For the
reasons given, the conclusion is that it would not.

Answer accordingly.
